items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News Can an E-Bike Replace Two Car Trips a Week? A Practical Route-Planning Checklist Reading Time: 3 minutes Can an E-Bike Replace Two Car Trips a Week? A Practical Route-Planning Checklist Replacing a car is a big decision. Replacing two familiar journeys can be a smaller, more useful experiment. An e-bike may suit a trip to work, a grocery pickup, or a visit to the library without needing to handle every journey in your week. The starting question is not “How far can this bike go?” It is “Which journeys can I repeat comfortably, legally, and with a workable backup?” This checklist helps turn that question into a practical plan rather than a promise about distance, money, or carbon savings. 1. Define the two trips you want to replace Look at an ordinary week and choose journeys you currently make by car. Start with predictable destinations, manageable loads, and flexible arrival times. An appointment with no margin for delay is probably not the easiest first attempt. Be clear about counting: an outward journey and its return are two one-way trips, but one round-trip outing. Write down which definition you are using. Two bike rides do not necessarily replace two car journeys if someone still drives the same route to collect you or your shopping. 2. Find the calmer route, not just the shortest Compare a cycling map with your knowledge of local streets. Look for lower-traffic connections, suitable crossings, and routes where you feel comfortable managing the bike. A small detour may be worthwhile if it avoids a difficult junction. Inspect the awkward details: where does a bike lane end, how do you cross a busy road, and is the destination entrance accessible? Check current local rules for your bike’s class and the roads or paths you plan to use. An app’s suggested route is not proof that access is legal or conditions are suitable. 3. Budget door-to-door time Allow time to unlock the bike, load bags, negotiate crossings, park, and get ready at your destination. Do not base your schedule on the motor’s assistance cutoff or a brief top-speed reading. Neither tells you the average speed of an entire journey. Try the route without an important deadline. Record the complete travel time and how it felt, then add a buffer appropriate to your schedule. 4. Plan battery use for the whole outing Include the return leg, any errands, and a reasonable detour. Advertised maximum range is not a dependable prediction for your route. Hills, wind, temperature, assistance level, load, battery condition, and other factors can change consumption. Begin with short, familiar rides and note battery use under your own conditions. Leave a conservative reserve rather than planning to arrive empty. If charging at work is part of the plan, confirm permission and a suitable location first. Follow the bike and battery manufacturer’s charging instructions; do not assume any available charger is compatible. 5. Solve parking and carrying before leaving Know where you can lock the bike at both ends. Check whether the parking arrangement works with the frame, your lock, and the property’s rules. If stairs or lifting are involved, assess whether you can manage the bike safely before relying on that access. Pack a realistic load for a practice ride. Secure bags so they cannot interfere with steering, wheels, or braking, and respect the bike’s and rack’s stated limits. Check tire condition and pressure, brakes, lights, and load security before departure. A lighter shopping trip may be a better starting point than a weekly household shop. For a practical example focused on weekend outings, FavoriteBikes’ guide to planning e-bike errands covers stop order, bags, cargo balance, and battery margin. Adapt those planning ideas to the trips you actually want to replace. 6. Decide when not to ride Choose your fallback before you need it. Transit, rescheduling, a lift, or using the car may be appropriate when conditions exceed your ability or the bike’s limits. Check transit rules in advance, including restrictions on e-bikes, batteries, and available carrying space. Rain, darkness, strong winds, snow, and ice can change the decision. Clothing and equipment do not make every route safe, and motor assistance does not remove traction or braking risks. Avoid an unsuitable route rather than treating two weekly trips as a target that must be met regardless of conditions. 7. Keep a simple two-week record For each attempt, note the journey replaced, door-to-door time, battery use, load, conditions, and any difficulty. Include the days you chose not to ride. Those decisions help reveal whether the plan works beyond an unusually easy day. If you compare costs, distinguish avoided fuel or parking from car expenses you still pay, and include relevant bike costs. Do not assign a fixed emissions saving to every ride: the result depends on the vehicle journey actually displaced and the comparison being made. Keep the routes that fit your life, revise the difficult ones, and leave room for other transport. The useful outcome is a repeatable choice—not a perfect score or a commitment to give up the car. The post Can an E-Bike Replace Two Car Trips a Week? A Practical Route-Planning Checklist appeared first on Happy Eco News .

items.descriptionOriginal: #thebetterindia Hyderabad is facing a serious water crisis. One of its main reservoirs has dropped to just 13%, and 6,000 water tankers are being booked every day. But what if the solution lies in a simple idea that helped Chennai fight its own water crisis? In 1995, Professor Sekhar Raghavan noticed something alarming. His tap water had turned salty because falling groundwater levels allowed seawater to seep in. Chennai received plenty of rainfall, but much of that water was going to waste. Instead of waiting for someone else to act, he began promoting rainwater harvesting. His idea was simple: collect rainwater from rooftops, driveways and other surfaces, filter it, and allow it to recharge underground aquifers. He cycled door to door, convincing residents to adopt the system. Many dismissed his efforts. But he persisted. In 2003, Tamil Nadu made rainwater harvesting mandatory in buildings. Groundwater levels reportedly rose by nearly 20 feet, helping Chennai improve its water security. For around 15 years, the city benefited from this approach. But there was a problem. Poor maintenance, clogged filters and neglected recharge pits weakened many systems. When Chennai faced another severe drought in 2019, the city once again came dangerously close to running out of drinking water. Today, Chennai is exploring solutions such as sponge parks and underground rainwater capture systems to strengthen its water resilience. The lesson? Rainwater harvesting isn't just about installing systems. It's about maintaining them, protecting groundwater and making every drop count. With Hyderabad facing mounting water stress, could Chennai's experience offer a way forward? Should Hyderabad make rainwater harvesting a bigger priority? items.titleOriginal: ‘Who Checks If Govt Officials Are Declaring Their Wealth Correctly?’: RTI Activist Explains 4 Key Steps

items.descriptionOriginal: Imagine a dozen people asked to write down what flats in the same apartment block are worth, and each gives a different figure. That is roughly what an IndiaSpend analysis found among Indian Foreign Service officers. At least a dozen of them had declared sharply different values for flats in the same apartment block in Delhi's Mayur Vihar. Each had filed a return as the rules demanded, yet the differences raised an important question: who was checking whether the values were accurate? "That gap between filing a declaration and proving it honest sits at the centre of how India tries to police the wealth of its public servants. Every public servant covered by the Lokpal law must declare assets and liabilities, but the form is only the first link in a longer chain of checks," explains L. Chakrapani, a Chennai-based RTI activist and former senior advocate at the Madras High Court . Someone has to read these returns, compare them with lawful income and act when the numbers don't add up. Here is how that chain is supposed to work, what the rules actually require today, and where it gets weak. What officials have to declare Under Section 44 of the Lokpal and Lokayuktas Act, 2013, every public servant covered by the Act is required to declare their assets and liabilities in the form and manner prescribed by the government. The original law required annual returns by 31 July and directed ministries or departments to publish the statements on their websites by 31 August, as set out in a Department of Personnel and Training order. However, the 2016 amendment replaced Section 44 and removed these specific requirements from the Act. Under the Lokpal and Lokayuktas Act, asset declarations were intended to help bring public servants' wealth under scrutiny. In December 2016, the Department of Personnel and Training (DoPT) said that returns under the amended Lokpal provision did not need to be filed until fresh rules were notified. In September 2022, it confirmed that those rules had still not been issued. Under the original Lokpal framework, the declaration covered the whole household. It included the assets and liabilities of the officer's spouse and dependent children. Officers of the IAS, IPS and Indian Forest Service already had a similar duty under the All India Services conduct rules, which ask for a return on first appointment. An India Today investigation reported that the return must list immovable property, shares, debentures, postal time deposits, cash including bank deposits, other movable property, and debts and liabilities. It also noted that the rules cover property held in an officer's own name, a family member's name, or anyone else's name. These service-specific requirements continue to matter even where the separate Lokpal declaration framework has been delayed. For example, IPS officers must file annual immovable property returns by 31 January under the All India Services conduct rules. Filing property returns creates a record against which an officer's wealth can be compared over time. Photograph: ( The Hindu ) That last part is telling. The rulebook also accounts for the possibility of officers holding wealth through other people, which is why the checks after the form matter as much as the form itself. Check one: Did the form even arrive? This is the simplest check, because authorities can identify who has failed to submit a required return. The Central Vigilance Commission has told central government officials that not filing property returns gives "good and sufficient reasons for instituting disciplinary action". It expressed deep concern over prolonged delays and in 2020 set 30 November as the deadline for 100% compliance. Even ministers have been late. Hindustan Times previously reported that 14 cabinet ministers and 21 junior ministers in a 77-strong council had not made their assets public, six weeks after the August deadline for declaring them to the Prime Minister. "There should be a mechanism to scrutinise the declarations. Otherwise there is a weakness that every later check tries to fix, since a filed form proves only that someone filled it in," Chakrapani says. The distinction matters. Treating a missing return as misconduct means officials can't wait for an investigation to begin before answering for the omission. Filing also creates a record to measure against later. "Filing gives authorities a baseline, because every later year can be compared with the one before it. Without that baseline, no one can say that wealth has grown faster than income, which is the question that the criminal law eventually asks," he explains. Check two: Are the numbers true? A form can be complete and still be wrong, which is why the differences reported in the Mayur Vihar declarations deserve scrutiny. IndiaSpend asked whether the real worry was that officers misstated values or "just don't care". For ordinary citizens, even seeing these forms has been a struggle. India Today reported that it took "two years of argument and persuasion" with the Department of Personnel and Training and the Central Information Commission, through the RTI route, to obtain just the immovable assets of around 120 secretary-rank officers. That was before the Lokpal Act originally introduced a requirement for ministries to publish annual statements. Although the 2016 amendment removed that requirement from Section 44, property returns filed under certain service rules are still published by the relevant departments. The Prevention of Corruption Act provides for action against public servants who cannot satisfactorily account for disproportionate assets. Photograph: ( Deccan Herald ) It shows why public access has always been part of the story. "Realistic verification rests on comparing declarations with independent records, mainly income-tax data, since the CBDT already cross-checks elected representatives' affidavits and reports any discrepancies. This rests on the CBDT and Election Commission framework, covered by the Lawyer E-News report, and on the CBDT's 2017 affidavit to the Supreme Court," Chakrapani tells The Better India. For elected representatives, the Central Board of Direct Taxes (CBDT) and the Election Commission of India (ECI) have a joint framework for verifying election affidavits. It allows asset disclosures to be checked against tax information and discrepancies to be investigated, according to a Supreme Court order reported by Lawyer E-News. In a September 2017 affidavit to the Supreme Court, the CBDT said it had begun investigating seven Lok Sabha members and 98 assembly members after finding discrepancies in their declarations. The Court had pulled up the government over members whose wealth showed "a massive jump". The department said details would go to the court in a sealed cover, since income-tax investigations are exempt under the transparency law. These checks concern election affidavits filed by candidates. They are distinct from the property returns filed by civil servants, although both raise the same question about independent verification. Check three: What if an official's wealth grows faster than their income? Once a discrepancy surfaces, the Prevention of Corruption Act gives investigators a legal test. The offence has a long history. Section 5(1)(e) of the 1947 Act criminalised property disproportionate to known income, and Section 13(1)(e) of the 1988 Act carried the idea forward before the 2018 amendment recodified it. Section 13(1)(b), as substituted by an amendment that took effect on 26 July 2018, makes it an offence to enrich oneself illicitly during the period of office. The law presumes illicit enrichment when a public servant, or anyone on their behalf, holds money or property disproportionate to known sources of income that they cannot satisfactorily account for. "The Act defines known sources of income as income from lawful sources, which means gifts, loans and savings count only if they can be shown to be lawful. A conviction carries imprisonment of not less than one year and up to seven years, and a fine," Chakrapani says. Tax records and independent financial checks can help investigators identify discrepancies between declared assets and lawful income. Photograph: ( The Hans ) The current Section 13(2) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, however, provides for imprisonment of four to ten years, along with a fine. The punishment was increased from the earlier one-to-seven-year range through an amendment effective from 16 January 2014. The Lokpal can act too. According to Nyaaya, its inquiry wing conducts an initial inquiry into corruption charges against a public servant, and the Lokpal can then file a case before a Special Court. PRS Legislative Research notes that the Lokpal holds power of superintendence over the CBI for cases it refers. This is where the declaration becomes evidence. It records what an officer owned on a given date and who else held property for the family. "A case can then succeed when investigators rebuild lawful income, loans, gifts and savings across the check period, and fail when that accounting has gaps," he says, drawing on his own litigation experience. Check four: Will the evidence hold up in court? Courts examine disproportionate assets cases in two stages. According to a legal analysis published by Casemine, the prosecution must first establish the disproportion. Only then does the burden shift to the accused to account satisfactorily for the assets. A High Court ruling reported by Taxguru shows how this plays out. The court set aside the conviction of two public servants in Chennai because the prosecution had not properly accounted for their legitimate income, loans, gifts and savings. It held that the defence had shown the properties came from lawful sources. Photograph: (AI-Generated) A strong case, then, needs more than a list of properties. Investigators must rebuild a full income and expenditure picture across the entire check period. According to Chakrapani, this is also why accurate declarations matter, since a truthful record of loans and gifts made years earlier can support or undercut a later explanation. Who is monitoring the growing wealth? The system has one gap that courts have already noticed. On 16 February 2018, a Supreme Court bench of Justices J Chelameswar and S Abdul Nazeer directed the creation of a permanent mechanism to monitor the assets of legislators that grow disproportionately to their known income. The bench said such assets "should alarm citizens and voters of any democratic society", according to LiveLaw. The Wire reports that the same bench refused a one-time investigation of named legislators, calling that "selective witch-hunting". It asked for monitoring of legislators whose assets rose by more than 100% by the next election, with findings reaching the appropriate legislature. Lok Prahari later filed a contempt petition, arguing that the government had not complied with several directions. The Wire reported on 24 April 2026 that the Supreme Court had disposed of the petition on 16 April 2026, after finding no wilful disobedience. The permanent mechanism had still not been created eight years after the original judgment. During the proceedings, the Union government pointed to an existing framework between the ECI and the CBDT for verifying asset disclosures. The Court accepted that contempt had not been established, bringing the proceedings to a close. In practice, that leaves verification to existing agencies, which act on complaints, tax discrepancies and criminal investigations. What this means for you The four checks show the different stages at which an asset declaration can be examined, although they do not necessarily follow one fixed sequence in every case. The first confirms that officials file, the second tests whether the numbers hold up, the third compares them with lawful income, and the fourth tests the evidence before a judge. A weak link anywhere can leave a questionable declaration unexamined. For citizens, the practical test is whether these stages are visible. Published returns, publicly reported verification findings and open court proceedings are among the ways outsiders can observe how the system is working. The Lokpal Act originally set the 31 July deadline, while other service rules continue to require property declarations. The Prevention of Corruption Act provides criminal penalties for illicit enrichment. The space between them depends on who is willing to read the forms. A declaration builds accountability only when someone checks it against income and acts on what they find. Eight years after the Supreme Court called for permanent monitoring of legislators' wealth, that mechanism remains absent. The question now is whether the existing checks can provide the scrutiny that the Court had sought. Sources ' Has Supreme Court Agreed to Bury its Own 2018 Mandate on Legislators' Assets?' : by for The Wire, Published on 24 April, 2026 ' The Lokpal and Lokayuktas Act, 2013 – Submission of declaration of assets and liabilities by the public servants ': by Department of Personnel and Training for gconnect.in (office memorandum) ' Section 13 in The Prevention of Corruption Act, 1988 ': by Government of India (as substituted by Act No. 16 of 2018) for Indian Kanoon, Published on 26 July, 2018 ' No Contempt Made Out Against Union For Not Creating Dedicated Cell To Monitor Legislators' Asset Growth: Supreme Court ': by [byline to confirm] for Lawyer E-News ' 7 MPs, 98 MLAs under I-T lens over assets declaration ': By Hindustan Times, Published on 12 September, 2017

items.title: Από τα δασικά βότανα σε μια επωνυμία 42 εκατομμυρίων Rs, πώς ένας αξιωματικός της IFS βοηθά τις οικογένειες των φυλών να κερδίσουν περισσότερα
items.titleOriginal: From Forest Herbs to a Rs 42 Crore Brand, How an IFS Officer Is Helping Tribal Families Earn More
items.description: Σε όλη τη Μάντια Πραντές, οι οικογένειες των φυλών έχουν μαζέψει βότανα και μέλι για γενιές, συχνά πουλώντας τα ελάχιστα. Ο αξιωματικός του IFS Gitanjali Janarthanan βοηθά στη σύνδεση της δουλειάς τους με μια ευρύτερη αγορά μέσω μιας υπάρχουσας μάρκας βοτάνων.
items.descriptionOriginal: Across Madhya Pradesh, tribal families have gathered herbs and honey for generations, often selling them for little. IFS officer Gitanjali Janarthanan is helping connect their work to a wider market through an existing herbal brand.

items.title: Οι επιστήμονες ανακαλύπτουν έναν κρυφό λόγο για τον οποίο οι μύες εξασθενούν με την ηλικία
items.titleOriginal: Scientists discover a hidden reason why muscles weaken with age
items.description: Οι επιστήμονες ανακάλυψαν έναν κρυφό αμυντικό μηχανισμό στους γερασμένους μύες που θυσιάζει τη δύναμη για να προστατεύσει τα κύτταρα από βλάβες. Στα ποντίκια, η μερική αποκατάσταση ενός κρίσιμου μορίου ανέστρεψε τα σημάδια μυϊκής απώλειας και απέτρεψε τον πρόωρο θάνατο, αυξάνοντας τις ελπίδες για νέες θεραπείες για τη μυϊκή μείωση που σχετίζεται με την ηλικία.
items.descriptionOriginal: Scientists have uncovered a hidden defense mechanism in aging muscles that sacrifices strength to protect cells from damage. In mice, partially restoring a crucial molecule reversed signs of muscle wasting and prevented premature death, raising hopes for new treatments for age-related muscle decline.

That’s why Etsy has taken definite steps to protect the almost 6 million artisan-entrepreneurs it hosts with new regulations against AI-generated content. “Our marketplace only works when buyers and sellers trust each other,” Etsy […] The post Etsy Cracks Down on AI-Generated Content to Protect Buyers from Barrage of Slop appeared first on Good News Network .

items.titleOriginal: Cashier Pays $150 for Homeless Mom and Toddler’s Groceries: “A Miracle,” She Said
items.description: Μια μητέρα που πίστευε ότι θα έπρεπε να φύγει από ένα μπακάλικο με άδεια χέρια συγκινήθηκε με κλάματα όταν ένας καλόκαρδος ταμίας μπήκε και πλήρωσε για τα παντοπωλεία της, δίνοντας σε εκείνη και τη μικρή κόρη της ένα λιγότερο πράγμα για να ανησυχούν σε μια δύσκολη στιγμή.
items.descriptionOriginal: A mother who thought she would have to leave a grocery store empty-handed was moved to tears when a kindhearted cashier stepped in and paid for her groceries, giving her and her young daughter one less thing to worry about during a difficult time.

items.descriptionOriginal: A 100th birthday usually calls for cake and candles, yet P Balasubramanian Menon, a lawyer from northern Kerala's Palakkad district, received something rarer and rather more formal. On 9 October 2026, six days before he turned 100 on 15 October, the Kerala High Court approved his designation as a Senior Advocate, timing the decision to coincide with the milestone itself. Chief Justice Soumen Sen began the initiative, and Bar and Bench reported that this might be the first time the court has conferred the rank on a lawyer who practises before the mofussil courts, which sit below the High Court. Bar and Bench calls Menon a trial lawyer, a practitioner who argues disputes before the courts that hear them first. Under Section 16 of the Advocates Act, 1961, India has two classes of advocates, senior advocates and other advocates. A High Court may formally designate an advocate as senior, with the advocate's consent, if it considers that ability, standing at the Bar or special knowledge or experience in law makes him deserving of the distinction. By approving the designation, the Kerala High Court formed that opinion about Menon after more than 76 years in practice. From Madras to Palakkad To understand the honour, it helps to look at where his career began and how it changed direction. Menon comes from a traditional family in Palakkad and studied law at Madras Law College before he began his career in 1950 at the Madras High Court , where he trained under Advocate General Kuttikrishnan Menon. After two years, he returned to Palakkad and worked under the criminal lawyer KS Ramakrishna Iyer. Bar and Bench's 2023 interview records that, like many lawyers of his generation, he had not made law his first choice. The Kerala High Court designated Menon a Senior Advocate on 9 October 2026, days before his 100th birthday. Photograph: ( Bar and Bench ) His early cases were criminal, but an encounter with a judge during a case in Kochi encouraged him to specialise in civil law, which has been his focus since 1952 and remains his main area of practice. LiveLaw reported in 2023 that he continued to practise on the civil side in his hometown. How 73 years of practising law earned him a world record His office, as Bar and Bench described it in 2023, has an old-world charm and countless mementoes, the latest being the Guinness World Record, while a second certificate in a glass frame marks the Indian Book of Records recognition that came a few months earlier. Guinness World Records verified his career in Kerala at 73 years and 60 days on 11 September 2023, making him the holder of the title for the longest career as a lawyer (male). Asked by Bar and Bench whether he had ever imagined such recognition, he said not even in his dreams. Menon surpassed the record set by Louis Triay, a Gibraltar lawyer whose record stood at 70 years and 311 days, according to LiveLaw. Triay died in February 2023 at the age of 94, months before Guinness World Records verified Menon's career. From beginning his career at the Madras High Court in 1950 to practising in Palakkad, Menon has spent decades arguing civil cases. Photograph: ( Facebook/Suma Kanakala ) PTI reported in November 2023 that, with the enthusiasm of a much younger lawyer, he went to his office and the courts every day without fail, met clients and kept his arguments and cross-examinations brief, even at 97. He describes his duty to clients in terms of trust, telling a television channel, "When a party approaches me with a case, he is coming by trusting me." At 100, he still has no plans to retire Three numbers recur in Menon's story, and each measures something different: his age of 100, his more than 76 years of practice according to Bar and Bench, and the 73 years and 60 days that Guinness verified on 11 September, 2023. The gap between the two shows his career continued well after Guinness took its measurement. In the 2023 interview, when he was in his 98th year, Menon said, "I am running 98. I am not even thinking of retirement." He added that he still works to earn his livelihood, and PTI noted that he smiles gently when anyone asks about retirement. The Senior Advocate rank now joins the Indian Book of Records certificate and the Guinness title among the formal recognitions of a career that began in 1950. Menon has said that he hopes the record can inspire others, and his story offers them a gentle lesson: a lawyer who keeps his arguments brief, answers to his clients' trust and smiles when asked about retirement has built the longest career Guinness has verified for a male lawyer, one patient year after another. Sources ' Kerala High Court confers Senior Advocate designation on 100-year-old P Balasubramanian Menon with longest law practice ': by Praisy Thomas for Bar and Bench, Published on 10 October, 2026 'I am not even thinking of retirement: Longest serving lawyer and Guinness World Record holder P Balasubramanian Menon ': by Sara Susan Jiji for Bar and Bench, Published on 16 November, 2023 ' At 97, Kerala man sets world record as longest serving lawyer ': by PTI for The Tribune, Published on 8 November, 2023 ' 97 Year Old Keralite Sets Guinness World Record As Lawyer With Longest Career ': by Navya Benny for LiveLaw ' Designation of Senior Advocates (Unstarred Question No. 489) ': by the Ministry of Law and Justice (answer by D V Sadananda Gowda) for Lok Sabha, Published on 26 February, 2015

items.title: Γιατί οι άνθρωποι ζωγραφίζουν τον εαυτό τους ως τίγρεις και χορεύουν στους δρόμους της Κεράλα και της Καρνατάκα
items.titleOriginal: Why People Paint Themselves as Tigers & Dance Through the Streets of Kerala & Karnataka
items.description: Πριν οι τίγρεις κατακτήσουν τους δρόμους του Thrissur, πρέπει να βαφτούν. Για ώρες, οι καλλιτέχνες καλύπτουν το σώμα των καλλιτεχνών με κίτρινες, μαύρες και κόκκινες ρίγες. Οι μάσκες συνεχίζονται, τα τύμπανα αρχίζουν να χτυπούν και την τέταρτη μέρα του Onam, οι «τίγρεις» χορεύουν μέσα στην πόλη της Κεράλα, περιπλανώνται και ορμούν πριν επευφημήσουν τα πλήθη. items.descriptionOriginal: Before the tigers take over the streets of Thrissur, they have to be painted. For hours, artists cover performers' bodies in yellow, black and red stripes. Masks go on, drums begin to beat, and on the fourth day of Onam, the 'tigers' dance through the Kerala city, prowling and pouncing before cheering crowds. These tigers are people, of course. But the animal they imitate has held a special place in local celebrations for generations. The tradition is called Pulikali, meaning 'play of the tigers'. And hundreds of kilometres away, along Karnataka's coast, another tiger dance carries stories of fear, admiration and protection. Together, these traditions offer a fascinating glimpse into how communities have understood and lived alongside the wildlife around them. How did tigers become part of Onam? Thrissur's Pulikali is believed to be around 200 years old. Its beginnings are often traced to Sakthan Thampuran, who ruled Cochin from 1790 to 1805. Historical accounts offer different explanations of how the dance developed, reflecting the many cultural influences that shaped Thrissur's public celebrations. Today, on Naalaam Onam, trained troupes gather with their bodies painted as tigers and leopards. They dance to the beats of traditional drums such as the chenda, thakil and udukku , sometimes acting out hunters pursuing tigers. Preparing for the performance takes hours of painting and practice. For the crowds that gather in Thrissur, the result is a celebration that brings the tiger into the heart of the city, year after year. Artists spend hours having their bodies painted in elaborate tiger or leopard patterns before dancing to percussion instruments such as the chenda, thakil and udukku. Photograph: (Manojk) Why do people in coastal Karnataka dance as tigers? Along Karnataka's coast, particularly in the Tulunadu region, a similar tradition called Pilivesha, also known as Hulivesha, brings painted tigers into the streets during annual celebrations. Performers paint their bodies in striking tiger patterns and dance through public spaces, keeping alive a tradition that has been passed down through generations. But what makes the tiger such an important part of these celebrations? The answer lies partly in the stories people have told about the animal for generations. In local folklore, the tiger has long represented strength, courage and protection. It has also been an animal people feared, particularly in places where communities lived close to forests. This relationship caught the attention of researcher Rohan Sharma. In a 2024 report for the Wildlife Conservation Society–India, Sharma spoke to performers, organisers and experts to understand Pilivesha's place in local life. His research explored how the tiger became a powerful cultural symbol and how stories about the animal have influenced the way communities understand wildlife. The dance offers a window into the beliefs, memories and traditions through which people have connected with wild animals for generations. Pilivesha documents a cultural relationship through which the animal occupies a place in community life beyond its biological presence in the landscape. Photograph: (Karthy shty) Can these dances change how we see wildlife? Admiring a tiger during a festival is different from encountering one near a village, where people may fear for their safety or livestock. There is no evidence that performing Pulikali or Pilivesha directly prevents conflict with wild animals. But these traditions remind us that people's relationships with wildlife have histories of their own. Sharma's research suggests that conservation efforts can benefit from understanding local beliefs and listening to communities, alongside protecting habitats and addressing real safety concerns. After all, people who have grown up hearing stories about tigers may understand the animal differently from someone who has encountered it only through books or documentaries. When the drums stop and the paint comes off, the festival ends. Yet the stories remain, passed from one generation to another. And perhaps that is where these tiger dances offer their most meaningful lesson. By understanding why communities have long feared, respected and celebrated the tiger, we can begin more thoughtful conversations about sharing our world with wildlife. Sources: 'Celebrating Nature-Culture Relationships: Documenting Cultures and Traditions of Tiger Folklore in Coastal Karnataka through the Annual Pilivesha Celebrations' : By Rohan Sharma, Published in 2024 'Sharing Spaces and Entanglements With Big Cats: The Warli and Their Waghoba in Maharashtra, India' : By Ramya Nair, Dhee, Omkar Patil, Nikit Surve, Anish Andheria, John D. C. Linnell, Vidya Athreya, Published on 23 June 2021 'Pulikali' : By Kerala Tourism

items.descriptionOriginal: As the wind gathers speed along Odisha's coast, preparedness begins long before the first tree falls or the first road floods. For a family living in a low-lying village, it could mean knowing which shelter to reach. For a pregnant woman, it could mean moving closer to a health centre before roads become impassable. Cyclone Arnab has caused extensive damage along the Andhra Pradesh coast, while parts of Odisha continue to experience intermittent rainfall and strong winds. The India Meteorological Department (IMD) has warned that the next 24 hours will be crucial, with the storm expected to move across Odisha towards southern Chhattisgarh, bringing heavy to very heavy rainfall and strong winds. The immediate priority is to protect lives. But Odisha's response also reflects a decade of learning to live with cyclones. What does that learning look like on the ground? When the warning turns into action The IMD has issued a red warning for six Odisha districts: Nabarangpur, Rayagada, Koraput, Malkangiri, Gajapati and Ganjam. Extremely heavy to very heavy rainfall, accompanied by strong winds, is forecast in these areas. The initial alert cited wind speeds of 50–70 kmph in the six districts, while broader forecasts for the affected areas have indicated the possibility of stronger winds. For now, the immediate task is to keep people away from dangerous coastlines, move vulnerable residents to safety and ensure rescue teams can reach those who need help. Photograph: (Odisha TV) Bargarh, Subarnapur, Boudh, Nuapada, Balangir, Kalahandi, Kandhamal, Puri, Khordha and Nayagarh are also expected to receive heavy to very heavy rainfall, with winds reaching 40–60 kmph. Here is what Odisha has done so far: Rail services have been disrupted, with more than 60 services reportedly cancelled across the affected network and others modified. Distant Warning Signal Number Two has been hoisted at Paradip and Dhamra ports, while Puri and Gopalpur ports have Local Cautionary Signal Number Three. Fishermen have been advised not to venture into the sea as conditions turn rough to very rough, with high seas expected along the southern Odisha coast. Schools and other educational institutions in affected areas have been closed, beaches shut to visitors, and restrictions on coastal road movement planned as part of the precautionary measures. The rescue teams waiting before disaster strikes One important part of cyclone preparedness is ensuring that help does not have to travel from scratch after the storm hits. Odisha has reportedly deployed 313 response teams: 60 Odisha Disaster Rapid Action Force (ODRAF) teams, nine National Disaster Response Force (NDRF) teams and 244 Fire and Emergency Services teams. Personnel from these agencies, alongside the police, have been positioned in vulnerable areas to respond to emergencies. For now, the immediate task is to keep people away from dangerous coastlines, move vulnerable residents to safety and ensure rescue teams can reach those who need help. But these preparations are part of a much longer journey, shaped by disasters that exposed the cost of inadequate warning systems and limited evacuation infrastructure. A decade of lessons, tested by every storm On 29 October 1999, a super cyclone struck Odisha's coast near Paradip with wind speeds estimated at 260–270 kmph. A storm surge more than 20 feet high, torrential rain, and widespread flooding battered coastal districts, washing away homes and cutting off communities from the outside world. Nearly 10,000 people died. Warnings did not reliably reach everyone who needed them, evacuation was limited, and there were too few shelters along the coast. In December 1999, Odisha established the Odisha State Disaster Management Authority. The Odisha Disaster Rapid Action Force followed in 2001, creating a specialised force for rescue and emergency response . Over the following years, disaster planning increasingly involved identifying vulnerable villages, mapping evacuation routes, building shelters and preparing communities before a storm arrived. The difference became visible in October 2013, when Cyclone Phailin approached the coast. The storm was powerful, with winds reaching around 200 kmph or more, but the response was markedly different from 1999. VIDEO | Cyclone Arnab: Visuals from Gopalpur Beach in Ganjam, Odisha (11:08 pm, Tuesday). (Full video available on PTI Videos - https://t.co/d8jp61yd2p) https://t.co/qWTTHHfRX1 — Press Trust of India (@PTI_News) October 27, 2026 Authorities evacuated more than one million people across Odisha and Andhra Pradesh, moving residents away from vulnerable coastal areas and into shelters and other safe buildings. In Odisha, the reported death toll was far lower than during the super cyclone, although fallen trees, damaged homes and disrupted infrastructure still left a substantial recovery effort. Six years later, Cyclone Fani offered another test. The IMD began tracking the developing storm days before it made landfall near Puri on 3 May 2019, giving authorities time to issue warnings and organise evacuations. More than 1.4 million people were evacuated in Odisha. Fani still caused widespread destruction, with powerful winds damaging homes, electricity infrastructure and trees, but the death toll was contained to dozens. What preparedness looks like for people on the ground The measure of preparedness must go beyond the number of people evacuated or rescue teams deployed. For a family living in a low-lying village, preparedness could mean knowing which shelter to reach. For a pregnant woman, it could mean moving closer to a health centre before roads become impassable. As Odisha braces for the storm, the immediate task is to ensure that warnings translate into action across vulnerable areas. Rescue teams must be able to reach those who need help, and residents must be able to move to safety before conditions deteriorate. A decade of cyclone learning is not a story of better forecasts or more teams on standby. It is measured in the time a family has to leave before floodwater rises, the distance a pregnant woman must travel to reach medical care, and whether a village can get help when roads are cut off. The storm may pass. For the people living in its path, the quality of preparedness can shape what happens for months afterwards. Sources: 'Odisha, Andhra shut schools, ban fishing as Cyclone Arnab nears; Centre stresses zero casualty' : By Press Trust of India, Published on 27 October 2026 'Cyclone Arnab impact: Red warning for six Odisha districts, heavy rain to continue' : By Poonam Singh, Published on 28 Oct 2026 'Cyclone Phailin triggers India's biggest evacuation operation in 23 years' : By Press Trust of India, Published on 12 October 2013 'Orissa super cyclone – A Synopsis' : By S.R. Kalsi, India Meteorological Department, Published in 2006

items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News When Humans Rise, Must Another Life Fall? Rethinking Human Interests and Animal Flourishing in an Anthropocentric World Reading Time: 4 minutes If human beings rise, must other life necessarily fall? We rarely ask because we’ve never learned to see beyond ourselves, understanding that cost starts with understanding how we imagined our place in the world. Human beings have become a species capable of deciding the fate of almost everything around us: deciding where forests remain, where roads are built, where rivers flow, where wildlife may move, which animals are confined, and which habitats are altered for human purposes. Yet the power to decide does not necessarily create a right to decide. Beneath these choices lies an anthropocentric hierarchy where human interests are treated as primary while the interests of other living beings are considered secondary whenever they conflict with human preferences. Against this hierarchy, I rely on Martha C. Nussbaum’s capabilities approach to examine whether human interests should automatically prevail when their pursuit restricts the fundamental capabilities of animals. In Justice for Animals: Our Collective Responsibility , Martha places animals in the sphere of justice and argues that justice requires more than preventing suffering. It requires securing the conditions necessary for animals to flourish according to their species-specific nature. The precise content of flourishing necessarily differs between each species. A bird requires opportunity to fly, a fish requires an aquatic environment in which it can swim and behave according to its nature, and a wild animal requires habitat, movement, ecological relationships, and the ability to exist without constant human control. For Martha, the problem is not simply suffering. It is capability deprivation. The human domination over animals is not accidental; it is structural and deeply embodied in our political, cultural, social, and economic systems. It does not arise merely from individual cruelty but from institutional arrangements designed around human benefits. Around the world, animal laws and conservation policies are structured within an anthropocentric framework. Animals are protected, conserved, and regulated not as right-bearing beings, but as resources to be managed for human benefits. Like, in Pakistan, animals are largely protected through welfare-based laws, not through a capabilities-based framework. The primary legislation, such as the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals Act, 1890 largely focuses on preventing visible cruelty rather than ensuring the flourishing of animals. Similarly, the provincial laws prioritize conservation of wildlife for human benefit rather than justice for animals themselves. The absence of a capabilities-based legal framework means that animals are still treated as objects of ownership and trade. Fish and birds sold on Pakistani streets are not perceived as beings whose rights are violated; instead, they are seen as commodities. They are viewed as property rather than beings of justice, where exploitation becomes habitual, invisible, and unquestioned. Human interests are not morally uniform. Human beings require food, shelter, health, security, transportation, livelihood, and infrastructure. But human societies also pursue convenience, entertainment, aesthetic preferences, commercial profits, and cultural habits. These interests cannot carry the same moral weight. A preference for cheap entertainment cannot automatically be placed on the same level as an animal’s basic freedom of movement. Fish trapped inside transparent plastic bags, under the complete control of a fish vendor on the streets of Lahore. Their aquatic life is reduced to a small plastic world where they remain alive, but are deprived of the space and freedom to live according to their nature. Photo by the author. Commercial tourism cannot automatically justify disturbing wildlife. Infrastructure development cannot justify destroying habitat where an alternative route or design is available. Martha’s framework, combined with necessity and proportionality principle, distinguishes the moral weight of different human claims. First, the human interest must be legitimate and sufficiently important. Secondly, the particular interference with animal capabilities must actually be necessary to achieve that interest. Lastly, where a less harmful and reasonable alternative exists, the more harmful practice should not be permitted merely because it is cheaper, easier, or customary. These tests distinguish human interests into non-essential, significant but non-vital, and vital human interests. Martha makes it clear that unnecessary human interests carry no moral or legal exception when they exploit an animal’s capabilities. Zoo confinement is a clear example of how entertainment and profit function as human interests that undermine animal rights. These animals are removed from their natural habitats and placed in artificial, restrictive environments, often in noisy and polluted urban settings. Zoos deny their freedom of movement, bodily integrity, and natural behavior’s, reducing them to spectacles for human amusement and revenue generation. The same analysis applies to the roadside sale of birds and fish. Birds confined in cages and fish sold in plastic bags are alive but incapable of flourishing. Even when sellers claim livelihood necessity, this interest remains non-essential because alternative businesses are available. The human right to business or livelihood cannot justify the exploitation of sentient beings. When business models depend on violating animal capabilities, they are illegal and should be prohibited. Justice requires banning such practices and supporting alternative livelihoods that do not rely on animal suffering. The commercial activities in protected wildlife areas reflect another form of human interest. Glamping and overcrowding disrupt wildlife migration patterns, feeding habits, breeding cycles, and freedom. While it generates profits, these benefits are not necessary for human survival and cannot justify the erosion of animal capabilities. Deforestation and unchecked urbanization also conflict with animals flourishing. They are built upon a hierarchy that privileges human expansion over interspecies justice. When forests and green belts are cleared for commercial use, animals lose the ecological foundation necessary for their existence. Habitat destruction fragments ecosystems, eliminates nesting and breeding grounds, and increases starvation and human-wildlife conflict. When forests are valued only for timber, and land and rivers are valued for commercial use, animals are reduced to externalities. In these cases, the principle is clear: human interest must be necessary and regulated. Economic gain, entertainment, and convenience cannot justify the deprivation of animal capabilities, particularly when alternatives exist or when such practices serve no essential human needs. If animal exploitation becomes normal and the state fails to regulate unnecessary human interests, the animal’s existence will become impossible. The limitation on human interests does not mean eliminating human freedom, but it means regulating and restricting activities that commodify living beings unnecessarily. Martha’s theory reminds us that animals are not objects of convenience; they are subjects whose capabilities impose limits on our ambition. The fish trapped in plastic, birds in cages, and zoo animals remind us that flourishing is a right, not a privilege, and human interest, no matter how convenient or profitable, must stop where the capabilities of other sentient beings begin. Limiting unnecessary and exploitative human interests is not a moral preference but a legal obligation in a just society committed to interspecies dignity and coexistence. It underscores that human freedom, while important, is not absolute and must yield when it conflicts with the flourishing of other species. The post When Humans Rise, Must Another Life Fall? Rethinking Human Interests and Animal Flourishing in an Anthropocentric World appeared first on Happy Eco News .

items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News Sustainable Polymers and Natural Rubber Chart a Path Toward Greener Materials Reading Time: 3 minutes Sustainable polymers and natural rubber are moving to the center of materials science, as new research shows how to design them to reduce their environmental footprint. Sustainable polymers and natural rubber took center stage at a joint symposium between researchers in France and Thailand. The University of Haute-Alsace and Kasetsart University co-hosted the online event across May 2026. The program covered a wide range of materials topics, from energy materials to nanotechnology. One theme stood out clearly across the sessions. Scientists are now designing polymers not just for performance, but for durability, repairability, and better end-of-life outcomes. Dr. Wirasak Smitthipong of Kasetsart University presented one of the symposium’s central ideas. His team studies smart polymers that respond to light and can heal themselves when damaged. These self-healing materials include rubber and hydrogel systems. Special molecular bonds allow damaged sections to reconnect and recover their function, much like scar tissue mending itself. That self-repair ability matters beyond the lab. If a material can signal damage and fix itself, it may not need replacing as often. This applies especially to coatings, adhesives, and composite products, where small damage often forces the replacement of a much larger item. Light also played a starring role in another presentation. Dr. Jacques Lalevée from the Institut de Science des Matériaux de Mulhouse, part of the University of Haute-Alsace, discussed new light-activated processing methods for high-performance materials. His work uses light to trigger chemical reactions in coatings, inks, adhesives, and 3D-printed parts. This approach offers precise control, produces little or no volatile organic compound release, and reacts faster than older methods. That same light-based technique can work with bio-based resins made from natural oils. This points toward manufacturing that uses less energy and allows for localized repairs rather than full replacement. Other researchers tackled the opposite end of a material’s life. Dr. Amornrat Lertworasirikul of Kasetsart University studies how to make polylactic acid, a common bio-based plastic known as PLA, break down more easily after use. PLA already appears in packaging, farming tools, and medical devices. Her team found that adding a small amount, just 3% by weight, of a plant-derived compound helped the plastic become more flexible and degrade faster in water. This research raises an important question for sustainable polymers and natural rubber alike. Should a material last for decades, break down quickly, or simply become easier to repair and reuse? The answer depends entirely on the product. Packaging that gets used once benefits from fast degradation, while structural materials benefit more from durability and repair options. Natural rubber also showed plenty of untapped potential. Sustainable polymers and natural rubber face the same fundamental design question: should a material last for decades, break down quickly, or be easier to repair and reuse? The new research shows that a 3% plant-derived additive can make plastic more flexible and water-degradable, suggesting the answer depends entirely on what the material is made to do. Photo by Lucas van Oort on Unsplash. Dr. Sutee Boonchui presented transparent, flexible films made by blending natural rubber with quantum dots, tiny particles that glow under light. These fluorescent films could improve road safety equipment, making traffic signs and markers more visible. The natural rubber base keeps the material flexible enough for real-world outdoor use. Medical safety also got a rubber-based upgrade. Dr. Kiadtisak Saenboonruang described multilayer gloves made from sustainable polymers and natural rubber, designed to block X-ray radiation more effectively. By layering in a nanoscale bismuth oxide additive, the gloves blocked more radiation than standard single-layer versions. The outer layers of pure natural rubber kept the gloves flexible and comfortable to wear. Tire manufacturing also came under the sustainability lens. Dr. Hassarutai Yangthong showed how fly ash, a waste byproduct from burning coal, can replace some of the zinc oxide typically used in tire rubber production. Zinc oxide use raises environmental concerns when it washes into waterways. Lifecycle analysis found that substituting fly ash lowered several measures of environmental harm, including toxicity to freshwater and marine life. Taken together, these projects reveal a shared philosophy. True sustainability depends on a material’s entire lifecycle, not simply whether it originates from renewable sources. A bio-based plastic that requires enormous energy to produce offers little advantage over conventional options. Likewise, a material that degrades too quickly may not suit long-term applications like construction or safety equipment. Sustainable polymers and natural rubber research is now moving toward this more complete picture. Scientists are learning to weigh performance, repairability, and lifespan together rather than treating them as separate goals. The symposium’s researchers plan to keep exploring how far these smart materials can go. As industries search for greener alternatives to conventional plastics and rubber, this kind of integrated thinking may prove essential to getting the balance right. The post Sustainable Polymers and Natural Rubber Chart a Path Toward Greener Materials appeared first on Happy Eco News .

items.descriptionOriginal: When architect Samruddhi S Chaphale took a group of construction workers to a park in Nagpur for yoga, their smiles stayed with her. "One day, I took some of the workers to a park in Nagpur and got them to do yoga," she recalls. "I could see how relaxed they became. There was a small smile on their faces, and that stayed with me." She had met workers who spent their days worrying about wages, their families and the dangers of their jobs. That visit made her consider how rarely anyone asked about their wellbeing. "I realised that many of them had never really stopped to celebrate their own lives. They were constantly thinking about work, earning their daily wages and getting through the day. Earlier, their attitude was often, 'Just give us the kit and let us go. We don't need anything else.' But I realised they needed much more than a safety kit. They needed someone to ask how they were doing." For Chaphale, founder of the Nagpur-based Levellers Foundation, this was a turning point. She began looking beyond the buildings she was trained to design, towards the people building them. When danger feels like part of the job Her concern began on construction sites, where she saw people working on roofs and at heights without adequate protective equipment. At first, she believed explaining the risks would help. "I realised that something was seriously wrong and extremely risky," Chaphale tells The Better India . "I would see workers doing roofing work without safety kits. Initially, I thought it was simply a matter of explaining to them why they needed the equipment. I would tell them to wear their safety gear, but many of them were not willing to. They would just say, 'Give us the kit and we will leave.'" As she spoke to more workers, she understood that providing equipment was only one part of the problem. Levellers Foundation has worked with organisations on awareness around welfare schemes, housing programmes and land rights. Photograph: (Levellers Foundation -Screengrab) "They had become so accustomed to risk that they had stopped thinking about their own safety. It wasn't that they didn't understand that something could go wrong. It was almost as if they had accepted that this was how their lives were going to be." Chaphale is an architect, educator and advocate for socially responsive design. Through Levellers Foundation's Project Salamati, she works with architects, doctors, activists and community organisations to address the lives and working conditions of construction and garden workers. A helmet helps protect a worker's head, but it cannot provide a toilet at the site. Gloves cannot ease years of back pain, and a safety briefing cannot resolve anxiety about wages or housing. Salamati's approach grew out of listening to these connected concerns. When pain threatens a day's earnings Construction workers lift, carry, bend and climb for hours. Over time, repetitive work and injuries can leave them with aching backs, damaged joints and fatigue. For someone who earns through physical labour, pain can mean missed work and less money at home. A 2016 study in the Indian Journal of Occupational and Environmental Medicine identified musculoskeletal disorders as a major occupational health concern and described them as the largest cause of work-related illness. There were burdens Chaphale could not see as easily. She knew of a construction worker whose wife had died. He still had to earn while dealing with loss and the responsibility of feeding his family. The site, and the need for an income, carried on. Mental health became an essential part of her work. A 2016 study of 404 male construction workers in Kolar, Karnataka found that 27.5% had probable psychological distress and 14.6% reported poor quality of life . The lowest scores concerned their surroundings, including living conditions, healthcare and recreation. In a 2023 study involving 75 migrant construction workers in India , researchers identified 64% as potentially needing psychosocial care. Among those surveyed, 83% reported feeling unhappy and nervous, 75% had sleep disturbances, 71% struggled to think clearly and 69% felt tired or had frequent headaches. Thirty-nine percent reported having thought about ending their lives. A 2016 study in the Indian Journal of Occupational and Environmental Medicine identified musculoskeletal disorders as a major occupational health concern and described them as the largest cause of work-related illness. Photograph: (Levellers Foundation-Screengrab) These were small, specific groups, so their findings cannot represent every construction worker in India. They do, however, point towards pressures that discussions about workplace safety can miss. Chaphale says Salamati's own screenings revealed distress too. "In one of our screenings, more than 80% of the workers screened positive for depression," she says. "One male worker was severely depressed." "They are dealing with physical pain, financial pressure, uncertainty, migration, difficult living conditions and the constant pressure to keep earning. We talk about whether they have helmets and gloves, but we also need to ask whether they are mentally okay." The questions women were beginning to ask For women on construction sites, Chaphale encountered concerns around washrooms, working hours, menstrual health and clothing. "I would see women working on construction sites where there were no proper washrooms," she says. "Some of them were working late into the night. They wouldn't necessarily complain about it because they had already accepted those conditions as normal." "I realised that sometimes I had to speak to the contractors because the workers themselves would not. They had normalised these conditions so much that they didn't always feel they could question them." Conversations about menstrual health required patience and trust. "There was almost no awareness around menstrual health among many of the women workers I interacted with," Chaphale says. "It was not simply about giving them information. We had to sit with them, talk to them patiently and understand their circumstances." View this post on Instagram A post shared by Levellers Foundation (@levellersfoundation) She also spoke to women who wore sarees while working. "I remember having conversations with women who were working in sarees and explaining that while a saree is what they are comfortable wearing, it may not always be practical or safe for certain kinds of physical work. I would tell them, 'Please consider wearing something that gives you greater mobility and safety, because your clothes can also become a risk at a construction site.'" She knew these discussions had to begin with understanding the workers' choices and circumstances. "You cannot walk into a community and tell people that everything they have been doing is wrong. You first have to build trust and understand why they do things the way they do. Once that trust develops, they start asking questions themselves." Soon, some women wanted her to reach others in their neighbourhoods. "They started telling me, 'Please come to our jhopadpattis [informal settlements] and talk to the other women too.' That was important for me because it meant that they were no longer just receiving information from us. They had started recognising these issues themselves and wanted other women to know about them." A safe place to live, and someone to care for the children Many workers Chaphale met had migrated to Nagpur and other cities from states including Madhya Pradesh and Bihar. Uncertain employment often went hand in hand with insecure housing. "They are migrant workers, and many of them live with the constant uncertainty that they could be asked to leave their settlement at any time," she says. "When you don't have secure housing, you are constantly fighting for your rozi-roti [livelihood]. You are thinking about where your family will sleep, and whether you will still have work tomorrow." India has a system of welfare boards for building and other construction workers, with protections now covered by labour codes that took effect in November 2025. According to the Union Labour Ministry , around 5.7 crore workers were registered with state and Union Territory welfare boards as of 30 June 2024. The boards had collected approximately Rs 1.15 lakh crore in cess and spent more than Rs 66,000 crore on benefits. But reaching those benefits can be complicated. "It is not enough to tell someone that a government housing scheme exists. We have to help them understand whether they are eligible, what documents they need, how they can register and what the process actually looks like." Levellers Foundation has worked with organisations such as YUVA to build awareness of welfare schemes, housing programmes and land rights, and to help workers register with Building and Other Construction Workers welfare boards. "For them, registration can become a gateway to a number of benefits," Chaphale says. "But if they don't know that these schemes exist or don't know how to access them, then the scheme might as well not exist for them." The foundation is also exploring childcare support. "We are now looking at a creche for the workers' babies because childcare is another issue that people don't think about. If both parents are working on construction sites, what happens to their small children? These are all connected problems." 'Their lives matter' One conversation with a 70-year-old worker showed Chaphale how deeply some workers had learnt to live with danger. "I once spoke to a 70-year-old worker about wearing safety equipment," she recalls. "I told him that he had to wear a safety kit because the work he was doing was dangerous." "He told me that he knew a friend who had fallen from a high-rise building and suffered a devastating head injury. And then he simply said, 'It is okay. These things can happen.'" "There is a kind of nonchalance that comes from living with risk for so long. They start believing that accidents are simply part of their lives. They don't always feel that their own lives are important enough to protect." Salamati is trying to challenge that acceptance of danger, while recognising that workers need support well beyond a construction site . "We want them to understand that their lives matter. Their health matters. Their safety matters", says Chaphale. Photograph: (Levellers Foundation-Project Salamati) "We want them to understand that their lives matter. Their health matters. Their safety matters. They deserve to go home safely to their families. They deserve healthcare, decent working conditions, housing and knowledge about their rights." A completed building may reveal the ambitions of a growing city. Its design shows how people will live and move within it. Behind it are the temporary shelters, missing toilets, workers balancing childcare and wages, ageing bodies still doing demanding work, and families unsure how long they can stay where they live. For Chaphale, the people who build India's cities deserve the same attention as the spaces they create. Their safety, health and dignity matter long after the building is finished.

items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News Bat Conservation Books Offer Something for Every Age Reading Time: 3 minutes From picture books for toddlers to a 400-page field guide, new bat conservation books invite readers of every age into the surprisingly wondrous world of the only flying mammal. Bat conservation books rarely dominate bestseller lists, but a fresh crop of titles released this year proves the subject deserves far more shelf space than it typically gets. Bat Conservation International recently rounded up a dozen standout titles spanning children’s picture books to dense scientific references, each aiming to replace fear of bats with fascination. For younger readers, several bat conservation books lean into storytelling and gentle life lessons. Stellaluna, considered among the first children’s books centered on bats, follows a baby fruit bat raised temporarily among birds after falling from her mother’s roost, ultimately learning that differences need not prevent friendship. I’m Not Scary follows a lonely bat who simply wants companionship despite living somewhere admittedly spooky, offering warm illustrations built around a familiar theme: kindness overcoming fear. Other bat conservation books for children tackle real conservation challenges directly. Bat Count: A Citizen Science Story introduces young readers to white-nose syndrome, the disease that has devastated North American bat populations, following a girl preparing for a community bat count who learns both the crisis facing bats and how ordinary people can help through citizen science. Amara and the Bats follows a similar arc, as a young bat enthusiast discovers her new neighborhood’s bat roosts have vanished due to tree removal, then finds inspiration in other young people already working to protect local bat populations. Additional titles for younger audiences round out the reading list. Little Red Bat explores the dilemma facing bat species that must choose between migration and hibernation as autumn arrives, weaving in facts about tree-roosting habits and camouflage along the way. The Bat Book, narrated from the perspective of a juvenile bat living under a bridge in Austin, Texas, directly addresses common misconceptions children repeat about bats being weird or scary. For adult readers and dedicated naturalists, bat conservation books shift toward deeper scientific territory. The Secret Lives of Bats follows renowned bat photographer and biologist Merlin Tuttle’s decades-long career, beginning with a teenage cave discovery outside Knoxville, Tennessee, that launched a lifetime devoted to bat ecology and conservation across encounters ranging from Kentucky moonshiners to charging elephants. The Weird and Wonderful World of Bats takes a curiosity-driven approach, devoting individual chapters to each bat sense, including echolocation, alongside candid explorations of bat mating behavior and social communication. For naturalists and dedicated readers, recent bat conservation books like Bats of the World: A Guide to Every Family and Bat Island document the diversity of nearly 1,500 known bat species through detailed photography, distribution maps, and firsthand field research. Photo courtesy of Bat Conservation International . The Genius Bat follows an ecologist’s research travels from Israeli deserts to tropical rainforests, examining how scientists design experiments to study bats’ extraordinary sensory and behavioral adaptations. For readers wanting comprehensive identification resources, bat conservation books like Bats of the World: A Guide to Every Family organize the roughly 1,500 known bat species by suborder, pairing close-up photography with distribution maps and details on diet, anatomy, and physiology. Bat Island narrows its focus dramatically, documenting the 76 bat species found on a single small island in Panama’s Lake Gatun through cinematic photography and firsthand research from Smithsonian Tropical Research Institute scientists. Rounding out the collection, Bats: An Illustrated Guide to All Species offers a 400-page reference dividing global bat diversity along modern phylogenetic lines, paired with extensive photography documenting species across every studied region. Together, these bat conservation books reflect a broader shift in how bats are represented in popular literature, moving decisively away from Halloween-season stereotypes toward genuine appreciation for animals that pollinate plants, disperse seeds, and consume enormous quantities of agricultural pests nightly. Whether introducing a child to their first bat-loving picture book character or offering seasoned naturalists a comprehensive species reference, this year’s releases make clear that meaningful conservation storytelling can also be genuinely engaging reading, proving that getting curious about bats might be the easiest first step toward protecting them. The post Bat Conservation Books Offer Something for Every Age appeared first on Happy Eco News .

items.title: Το πείραμα του Business School χωρίς τιμές
items.titleOriginal: The Business School Experiment with No Prices
items.description: Νωρίς στο σχολείο, ο Gaurav Marathe αγκάλιασε ένα μάντρα Viraja που μεταφράστηκε από έναν δάσκαλο: "Οι άνθρωποι είναι σαν ένα κερί. Αφού καεί το κερί, ο άνθρακας μένει πάνω του, και πρέπει να αφαιρέσετε αυτόν τον μαύρο άνθρακα από το φως, ώστε το φως να ανάψει ξανά." Το μάντρα του έμαθε να πειραματίζεται τόσο με την αφαίρεση του άνθρακα όσο και με το φωτισμό του jyoti -- το φως…
items.descriptionOriginal: Early on in school, Gaurav Marathe embraced a Viraja mantra translated by a teacher: "Humans are like a candle. After the candle burns, carbon stays on it, and you have to remove that black carbon from the light so the light again illuminates." The mantra taught him to experiment with both removing the carbon and illuminating the jyoti -- the light that exists within. In one of many experiments, he challenged students to remove the carbon of a task-driven, rule-driven festival on a campus where he taught. "Let's do that experiment. Let it be the kind of carnival where nobody is charging anything. No cost price, nothing. If anybody wants to pay, they pay. If they don't, they don't. Let's believe in that spirit." It was successful beyond anyone's imagination, and became a "Soul Carnival" where the focus is on giving over profiting. "Perhaps that's the point of these experiments — not to have all the answers, but to keep creating spaces where we can go close to inner jyoti a little more."

items.description: Μια νέα κλινική δοκιμή δείχνει ότι ένα απλό καθημερινό συμπλήρωμα φυτικών ινών θα μπορούσε να μειώσει σημαντικά τον πόνο της οστεοαρθρίτιδας στο γόνατο, να βελτιώσει τη μυϊκή δύναμη και να κάνει το σώμα λιγότερο ευαίσθητο στον πόνο. items.descriptionOriginal: A new clinical trial suggests that a simple daily fiber supplement could significantly reduce knee osteoarthritis pain, improve muscle strength, and make the body less sensitive to pain. Researchers discovered that the benefits may be linked to changes in gut bacteria and the hormone GLP-1, revealing a promising new approach to arthritis relief.

items.descriptionOriginal: A curled leaf, a handful of clay and a shallow depression in the earth have become the starting point for an unusual water conservation experiment in the forests of Keonjhar district. The idea is: can children learn to hold on to water by observing how nature does it? A lesson hidden in a leaf On a walk through the dry forest slopes around Haladipani, a village in Odisha's Keonjhar district a local elder stopped beside a curled sal leaf. Inside its cupped surface, a thin film of dew had collected, holding on to moisture even as the surrounding ground dried in the heat. For the children accompanying him, it was a small observation with a larger question behind it. If a leaf could catch and retain a little water, could they recreate that ability on the ground, where water was harder to come by? The elder, known locally as the 'jungle master', encouraged them to try. Instead of using plastic sheets or manufactured containers, the children began experimenting with sal leaves and clay to make small pits that could collect and retain water. View this post on Instagram A post shared by Village Square (@villagesquareindia) The experiment was documented by Biswabijayini Mohanty in a report published by Village Square on 16 September 2026, titled A Lesson in Water Conservation from a Leaf . The report describes how an observation made during a forest walk developed into a practical exercise in water conservation, with the children learning through trial, error and close attention to their surroundings. How the children made the pits The children dug shallow depressions near the forest edge using simple tools, sticks and their hands. But they soon encountered a problem: the loose soil absorbed the water poured into the pits before it could remain there for long. The jungle master helped them rethink the design. First, they laid broad sal leaves across the bottom and sides of each depression, overlapping them like roof tiles . They then spread clay soil over the leaves, pressing and smoothing it until the hollow took the shape of a shallow bowl. The two materials served different purposes. The leaf layer helped support the clay as it dried, while the compacted clay formed a lining intended to slow the movement of water into the surrounding soil. The children repeated the process, allowing the clay to set before filling the pits. Within about two weeks, they had created a network of small water-holding depressions along the forest edges. According to Village Square, the pits were generally no deeper than a forearm and rarely wider than a large dining plate. There was no plastic lining , costly equipment or elaborate construction involved. The materials came from the landscape around them, and the method evolved through observation and experimentation. When the rains put the idea to the test The pits were intended to hold water during the dry months. But after several days of rain, runoff carried loose soil down the slopes, turning surrounding water sources muddy. The pits, however, appeared to retain relatively clearer water. According to Village Square, the pits were generally no deeper than a forearm and rarely wider than a large dining plate. Photograph: (Gadadhar Dehury-Via Village Square) The explanation lies partly in the way water behaves when it is allowed to settle. Rainwater flowing over exposed ground can carry suspended particles of soil and other sediment. When that water collects in a relatively still depression, heavier particles can gradually settle at the bottom, leaving the water above them less cloudy. The report also records visits by wildlife, including barking deer, rabbits, mongooses and squirrels, which were seen drinking from the pits. There is an important distinction, however, between water that looks clear and water that is safe to drink. The report does not provide laboratory test results establishing the potability of water collected in these pits. What science tells us about sal leaves and water The principle behind the experiment has parallels in traditional agricultural practices documented elsewhere in Odisha A study compiled by Dr Prasanta Kumar Mishra, a principal scientist at the Central Research Institute for Dryland Agriculture, describes how tribal farmers in Pakanagaon village in Kandhamal district use sal leaves as mulch in turmeric fields. The account, published by LEISA India, notes that farmers spread a layer approximately 20–25 cm thick over their fields before the monsoon. The leaf cover helps conserve soil moisture, reduce runoff and soil loss, suppress weeds and protect the soil from the direct impact of raindrops. Mulching works by covering the soil surface, reducing its exposure to direct sunlight and wind and helping slow evaporation. It can also reduce the force with which raindrops strike the ground, limiting the displacement of soil particles. Depending on the soil and rainfall conditions, this cover can allow more water to remain available in the soil. The Haladipani experiment uses sal leaves differently: rather than spreading them over agricultural land, the children place them beneath a compacted clay lining in small depressions. Both of these practices show how locally available sal can be used to manage moisture and soil. The children are not simply being told that water is scarce or that forests must be protected. They are being encouraged to observe a leaf, understand what it does, test an idea and learn from what happens next. It is a practical starting point for environmental learning. Sources: 'Farmers' practices of improving soil health by mulching in semi-arid india' : By Dr Prasanta Kumar Mishra 'Ground Report-A lesson in water conservation from a leaf' : By Biswabijayini Mohanty, Published on 16 September 2026

items.description: ΑΠΟ ΤΗΝ ΚΑΘΗΜΕΡΙΝΗ ΣΥΝΤΑΚΤΙΚΗ ΟΜΑΔΑ OPTIMIST Αυτό το άρθρο ξεκινά τη σειρά Local Changemakers 2026 του The Optimist Daily, δίνοντας έμφαση στους δημιουργούς αλλαγής 30 ετών και κάτω.
