Ο πατέρας του ετοίμαζε τις βαλίτσες του για ένα ταξίδι αποστολής στην Κένυα, όπου ήταν εθελοντής με την Kenya Relief , έναν ιατρικό οργανισμό που διευθύνει ένα scho…
items.descriptionOriginal: BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM This article kicks off The Optimist Daily’s Local Changemakers 2026 series, spotlighting changemakers 30 and under. It was winter break, and Dilan Mehta had time on his hands. His dad was packing for a mission trip to Kenya, where he’d been volunteering with Kenya Relief , a medical organization that runs a school in Migori, for years. Dilan packed a bag of stuffed animals for the children there. Then he glanced at his 3D printer. He started designing LEGO-inspired sets, printing each one out, and tucking them in alongside the stuffed animals. Somewhere between one print and the next, a different thought took shape. The school had students who could use a curriculum, and his dad had room in a suitcase. That’s how a 3D printer ended up in Migori, Kenya, and why it’s still being used to teach students today. What is Student Makers? Student Makers is a nonprofit that offers free STEM workshops to students across the United States, Kenya, and India, and every instructor is a former student. Most of them are still in high school. The organization was founded in California in 2019 by Anthony Neil Tan, then a high school senior. There was no space at his school where students interested in technology and making could come together to learn, so he built one. He called it the Maker Hub Club Initiative, secured a $5,000 grant from a social impact scholarship, and got it off the ground. The framework was three steps: learn a skill , make a project, showcase it. He was in his first year of college when he started handing it off. Serve: the fourth pillar Dilan didn’t find Student Makers; rather, Anthony found him. Roughly six years ago, Dilan was only in 8th grade and had entered an Autodesk design contest with a 3D-printed fingerboard, one that used flexible filament on the grip surface to behave like rubber. Anthony came across it and reached out. Would Dilan want to join a group where students build things and learn from each other? He joined, took the 3D printing course, came back as an instructor, and eventually rebuilt the entire curriculum from scratch around design thinking rather than output. A few years later, he was running the organization. But he felt that the project’s mission needed some rethinking. The original framework had three steps: learn, make, showcase. Dilan added a fourth, serve, because the workshops were primarily reaching students who already had resources, and that wasn’t what he’d signed up for. His dad’s Kenya-bound suitcase gave him the opening for a bigger idea to launch. Teaching through rain and static When Dilan sent that 3D printer to Kenya Relief Academy, he wasn’t thinking about it as a program. He was thinking about a school with 800 students, roughly 170 to 190 of them orphaned children, consistently ranked the top primary school in its region out of more than 800, and without any STEM infrastructure. His dad’s Kenya Relief contacts connected him to the teachers there, and he started meeting with them remotely three times a week. Every session ran over video call, Dilan in the US and the teachers in Migori, and when the Wi-Fi dropped, which it often would, they’d wait, reconnect, and keep going. He trained them in Autodesk Fusion 360, Tinkercad, and 3D printer operation, working through how to teach all of it to a classroom he’s never seen in person. “They constantly have Wi-Fi issues,” Dilan said. “Anytime there’s rain, they basically lose connection. Just being patient, being empathetic , understanding that that’s just the situation.” Ruth Agongo, a teacher at Kenya Relief Academy, described what it looked like from the other end. “You are a game-changer,” she said. “Whatever you have taught us, we are putting into action because the kids are really excited by the technology.” Jacob A few semesters into his time at Georgia Tech, once Dilan had actually taken a step back from Student Makers and was serving mostly as an advisory board member, Dilan got a message from the teachers at Kenya Relief Academy. They needed help with a science fair project: an Arduino-based robot that could navigate a garden, measure soil moisture at different points, and decide where to water. Dilan didn’t know much about robotics, but he was at Georgia Tech, so he asked around. Twelve students from the university ended up on the project. They built components in Atlanta while the Kenya team built in Migori, troubleshot over video call, and sent physical supplies through a similar suitcase network that had carried the original printer. That team placed third at regionals of the Kenya Science and Engineering Fair. One of the students on it, a ninth-grader named Jacob, now leads Kenya Relief Academy’s robotics team. His dream is to become a rocket engineer at NASA. A family connection in India Rohan Naegle, who led Student Makers before the current team took over, brought a similar program to Dr. R.V. Shah English Medium School in rural Gujarat, India, after his grandfather put him in touch with the school. Live 3D printing classes run there over video call, using the same structure. More than 25 secondary students have completed the program, and a donated printer stays at the school. Both the Kenya and India connections came organically, through family. How the pipeline runs Aarush Goel, who now leads the high school chapters, came in the same way Dilan did: a friend pulled him in to co-teach a Python workshop, and he showed up not entirely sure what he was doing. “You just start teaching and everything goes into place,” he said. He’s since led five workshop tracks across the US, and next year he’ll start a Student Makers chapter at his own college. Instructors are recruited the same way at every level. At the end of each cycle, a call goes out for anyone who wants to come back and teach the next round. Usually one or two students say yes. They already know the program from the inside, which tends to make them good at the part that matters most: building something new students actually want to stay in. Anthony, watching from his current advisory role, put it plainly. “It’s more relatable, a high schooler showing a middle schooler how to do some 3D printing than someone who’s already a young adult,” he said. “So it’s nice keeping that peer-to-peer instruction model.” He’s 25. The organization he started as a high school senior just turned seven. Growing the network Student Makers recently joined a partnership with Youth Technology Corps Global Alliance , a network of schools across roughly 12 countries that has been running a similar peer-learning model since 1998. YTC has been doing this for nearly three decades and has school connections worldwide; Student Makers brings the volunteers and the curriculum. This fall, programs are launching under the partnership in Mexico, Colombia, Ethiopia, and Illinois, with the 3D printing and CAD curriculum going into Mexico specifically. “I would have never imagined that we would have this extensive of a reach,” Anthony said. The reach he couldn’t have imagined started with a simple observation: students interested in technology and making didn’t have a space to come together. So he built one. Why Student Makers opens this year’s series Each year, The Optimist Daily’s Local Changemakers series runs in the weeks before Thanksgiving, and this year, for the first time, every person in it is 30 or under. When Aarush reached out to us with the Student Makers story last summer, we spent weeks talking with the people who built this organization and were honestly floored by their dedication, hard work, and willingness to serve others. The five other changemakers in this year’s series were nominated by The Optimist Daily community, but Student Makers was not. It was the story that inspired the decision behind this year’s “30 and under” theme. This article skims the surface of the deeper story behind Student Makers. If you want to learn more about their incredible work, hang tight for a podcast episode featuring the voices behind this initiative. It’ll be coming out in early 2027. In the meantime, you can learn more and support their work at www.studentmakers.org . The post Student Makers, a deeper dive: bringing free STEM to students on three continents first appeared on The Optimist Daily: Making Solutions the News .

Συμπληρώνετε μια φόρμα, τσεκάρετε ένα πλαίσιο, εξηγείτε τις περιστάσεις σας σε κάποιον που έχει εξουσία για το αποτέλεσμα. Βίβιαν Χ…
items.descriptionOriginal: BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM This article is part of The Optimist Daily’s Local Changemakers 2026 series, spotlighting changemakers 30 and under. Most social programs ask you to declare yourself before they’ll give you anything. You fill out a form, check a box, explain your circumstances to someone with authority over the outcome. Vivian Ho built All The Same Organization around the idea that this moment, identifying yourself as someone who needs help, was what kept people from asking at all. Vivian lives in Cedar Park, Texas, but the organization operates nationally. She is, remarkably, only 17 years old. ATS delivers supply packages directly to low-income families through Title I schools: food, hygiene products, household necessities, school supplies. Families request what they need through an anonymous sign-up system. No one who receives support is required to name themselves as the recipient. “Just because resources exist does not mean that it’s accessible,” wrote Anika Luangaphay, who co-founded ATS alongside Vivian. The anonymous system, Luangaphay explained, was designed to let families “choose what type of support they want” without attaching their identity to the request. Volunteers with the All The Same Organization Reaching Title I families across the country Since its founding, ATS has grown to more than 200 chapters with roughly 8,000 volunteers and has distributed over 150,000 supplies to families at Title I schools. In a single back-to-school season , the organization served five schools and delivered more than 15,000 school supplies. Vendor events in the Austin and Cedar Park area have raised more than $75,000 in goods. ATS brings supplies directly to schools, removing the need for families to travel. Outreach is conducted across language barriers so that immigrant families can find and navigate the program without information being another wall to get over. Aoto Yamazaki, a longtime volunteer, described Vivian’s approach as incredibly empathetic and well-thought-out: “What makes Vivian’s work especially meaningful to me is how intentionally she considers each student’s culture due to her past experiences as an immigrant.” Cultural Surprises Cultural Surprises works like this: volunteers research the cultural background of a recipient family, then create handmade arts and crafts based on what they find. The crafts go out alongside the supply packages. More than 500 crafts have been made for over 60 recipients. Volunteers don’t just pack boxes; they do the work to understand the people they’re packing for. Yamazaki wrote that the program had changed what he understood about volunteering: “Being part of this work has taught me so much about cultures I previously knew little about, including Hmong culture.” Luangaphay connected it directly to Vivian’s own history. “She had told me herself that she grew up suppressing her culture due to being a Vietnamese immigrant,” Luangaphay wrote, “so now she recognizes the students in Title I schools often neglect their own culture, too.” The crafts are partly a way of giving back something that growing up between cultures tends to cost. ATS has now secured funding for a Cultural Spotlight Scholarship. Rather than asking volunteers to make crafts for recipients, this program invites students to create art and crafts inspired by their own cultures, with a short written description of what the piece means and where it comes from. Those descriptions get shared with a wider audience. Winners will receive $1,250. The goal, as Luangaphay described it, is to give participants “a deep dive into a culture, whether it’s their own or another person’s.” A classroom, and what came after After noticing a gap in career exposure at the schools she worked with, Vivian fundraised for medical supplies, including mannequins, suture kits, and stethoscopes, then developed a partnership with Age of Central Texas to build a functional medical classroom at Dobie Middle School. When the school went through a turnaround and that classroom was shut down, she turned her attention to other Title I schools rather than walking away. “Her willingness to keep finding ways to help, even when her original efforts did not go as planned, is something that has always stayed with me,” Yamazaki wrote. Yamazaki saw the same thing in smaller moments. Early in his time with the organization, he told Vivian he wanted to start his own project after being inspired by her work. “She selflessly gave me her time, advice, and guidance, walking me through how to turn my ideas into something that could create a real impact,” he wrote. She was, at that point, a teenager running a multi-chapter national nonprofit. Vivian received two nominations for this series: one from her co-founder and one from a volunteer she inspired to build something of his own. Both of them described an organization built on one idea: that people should be able to ask for help without giving anything of themselves away to get it. Learn more and get involved at www.allthesame.org . Vivian Ho, founder. The post Meet Vivian Ho: the 17-year-old who built a supply network around dignity, not charity first appeared on The Optimist Daily: Making Solutions the News .

items.title: Η πιο στοιχειωμένη Αμερική; 7 πόλεις με τρομακτική φήμη
items.titleOriginal: America’s Most Haunted? 7 Cities With Seriously Spooky Reputations
items.description: Από τον βαθύ Νότο έως την αποικιακή Νέα Αγγλία, ορισμένες τοποθεσίες των ΗΠΑ έχουν αποκτήσει ανατριχιαστική φήμη για αναφορές εμφανίσεων και άλλης παραφυσικής δραστηριότητας. Οι μακριές σκιές έχουν δημιουργηθεί από ιστορίες βουτηγμένες στην καταστροφή, και αφθονούν οι ιστορίες ανήσυχων ψυχών καταδικασμένων σε νεκροταφεία και θλιμμένων poltergeists με κόκαλα να διαλέξουν. Πολλές από αυτές τις πόλεις r…
items.descriptionOriginal: From the deep South to colonial New England, certain U.S. locales have developed chilling reputations for reports of apparitions and other paranormal activity. Long shadows have been cast by histories steeped in calamity, and stories abound of restless souls condemned to cemeteries and peevish poltergeists with bones to pick. Many of these cities relish their notoriety, with multiple laying claim to the title of most haunted in the country. We detail a few of them below, but whether you use this list as a roster of places you dare not enter or as a resource for your next vacation, proceed with caution: We can’t promise that reading our roundup won’t summon the spirits mentioned within it. Savannah, Georgia Glen Richard—iStock/Getty Images Plus Savannah offers all the charm of the South and all the unease of a Southern Gothic novel — if you know where to look. Lurking amid the oak-lined streets and majestic mansions are specters borne of centuries of tragedy (or so the story goes). Founded in 1733, the city played major roles in the Revolutionary and Civil Wars and was ravaged by several yellow fever outbreaks in the 1800s. The souls lost in those events are said to haunt Savannah’s historic cemeteries and buildings. “Visitors and locals alike report unexplained phenomena across Savannah: sudden cold spots, shadow figures, voices, apparitions, and objects moving without cause,” claims local hotel Bellwether House, which was built in 1876. “Ghost sightings aren’t confined to one building — they’re woven into the city itself.” Even its own chamber of commerce boasts its reputation as “the most haunted city in America” (a title New Orleans also claims). Check out 10 of the spookiest places in Savannah. Atchison, Kansas DonsESLAdventure—iStock Editorial/Getty Images Plus Known for being the birthplace of Amelia Earhart , Atchison’s other claim to fame is its purported paranormal activity. Situated on the Missouri River, it’s home to the infamous Sallie House . Legend has it that after a young girl named Sallie died there during a failed appendicitis operation in 1905, her ghost stuck around. Though locals had long considered the abode haunted, the story truly took hold in 1993 when a couple moved in and began experiencing ominous phenomena — including a fire, objects moving around on their own, and unexplained scratches. Other eerie sites in Atchison (called “America’s most haunted town” by its tourism department) include the McInteer Villa , an 1889 Victorian mansion that’s elicited reports of supernatural occurrences; the Rose Trunk Building , where visitors have claimed they sensed an unseen presence; and Benedictine College, said to be haunted by the spirits of monks who founded it over 150 years ago. New Orleans, Louisiana lightphoto—iStock/Getty Images Plus Welcome to New Orleans, a 308-year-old city rife with historical trauma. Its early days were marked by violence and sorrow, which continued into the 19th century as slavery, the Civil War, and several disease outbreaks took their toll. A merging of West African spiritual practices and Catholicism gave rise to its distinct voodoo tradition , and today, “the line between the living and the dead often feels surprisingly thin,” per the city’s tourism department. If you’re looking for a hair-raising time, you should certainly visit the French Quarter. Book a stay at the Andrew Jackson Hotel — believed to be haunted by five boys who perished there in a fire when it was a boarding school — or dine at Antoine’s Restaurant, reportedly home to 19th-century spirits who peer out from the bathroom mirrors. The ghost of author William Faulkner is said to remain in the rooms he rented in the neighborhood, which have since been converted into a bookstore called Faulkner House Books. Learn about more haunted places in New Orleans. Salem, Massachusetts AndTheyTravel—iStock Editorial / Getty Images Plus Salem’s dark history has seemingly cast a spell over the colonial New England town. The area’s notorious witch trials saw around 200 people accused of witchcraft in the 1690s. About 30 were found guilty and at least 19 were put to death. Today, this chilling past resurfaces in reports of ghost sightings and other supernatural phenomena. Proctor’s Ledge , the trials’ primary execution site, is said to be haunted, with visitors reporting cold spots, incandescent orbs, and a disembodied voice, per Ghost City Tours. The Joshua Ward House , built on the site where George Corwin — High Sheriff during the witch trials — once lived, is also the stuff of legend: An accused man named Giles Corey is rumored to have cursed Corwin and the town of Salem with his final breath during his execution. At the Old Burying Point Cemetery , established in 1637, condemned souls are believed to be responsible for mysterious shadows, noises, mist, and an overwhelming sense of despair. Anoka, Minnesota Officially known as “the Halloween Capital of the World,” Anoka is rich with tales of the paranormal. Reportedly haunted buildings include the Anoka State Hospital , a psychiatric institution that opened in 1900; Colonial Hall, where furniture is said to move around inexplicably after dark; and the old Anoka library, with a known history of “books flying off of shelves,” per local outlet HometownSource. The Anoka County Historical Society, which formerly used the library as its headquarters, offers guided ghost tours that are “60% history, 40% folklore” and based on real stories from the people who live and work in the city’s buildings. Virginia City, Nevada NNehring—E+/Getty Images “To say everything is haunted in this old mining town is not too far from the truth,” proclaims Virginia City’s tourism department. The locale topped the ranking in the 2026 Spookiest Cities Report , a playful analysis by home security company Vivint. The ranking used seven measures, adjusted for population: haunted places, ghost sightings, funeral services, haunted houses, psychics and astrologers, spiritual shops, and spooky Google search volume. Visitors can explore eerie places like the Gold Hill Hotel, Nevada’s oldest, where rumors persist of children’s ghosts running the halls, or bring home a bottle of Cemetery Gin, the city’s own distilled spirit. This month — dubbed Hauntober — one of the area’s top ghost experts is leading paranormal investigations at the historic St. Mary’s Art Center, which was originally a hospital and is known as one of Virginia City’s most haunted buildings. Gettysburg, Pennsylvania pabradyphoto— iStock/Getty Images Plus The Civil War’s Battle of Gettysburg in 1863 resulted in over 50,000 casualties, and many believe that the spirits of the soldiers who died on the battlefield remain there, reliving the brutal conflict. For over 100 years, visitors and locals have reported “phantom footsteps, ghostly drumbeats, and echoes of musket fire and cannon blasts,” per History . Other spots in the city, widely known as one of the country’s most haunted places , have their own eerie history tied to the war. The Jennie Wade House Museum commemorates, and is said to be possessed by, the only civilian killed in the battle. Visitors have claimed to hear whispers, feel cold spots, and see Wade’s ghost floating through the rooms. Those daring enough to walk into the Sachs Covered Bridge — where a trio of Confederate soldiers were executed for impersonating Union troops — may encounter three disembodied heads or feel phantom fingers tapping their shoulders.

items.titleOriginal: New Simulation Offers Unprecedented Look at the Universe’s First 2 Billion Years
items.description: Τι συνέβη μετά το Big Bang; Μια ομάδα φυσικών, αξιοποιώντας τα διαστημικά τηλεσκόπια James Webb και Nancy Grace Roman, εργάζονται για να οπτικοποιήσουν την απάντηση σε αυτή την ερώτηση χρησιμοποιώντας μια νέα προσομοίωση υπολογιστή που ονομάζεται Lumina. Και μοιράζονται μερικές υπέροχες εικόνες και βίντεο στη διαδικασία. Μια νέα μελέτη από το Κέντρο Χάρβαρντ και Σμιθσόνιαν…
items.descriptionOriginal: What happened after the Big Bang? A team of physicists, harnessing the James Webb and Nancy Grace Roman space telescopes, are working to visualize the answer to that question using a novel computer simulation called Lumina. And they’re sharing some pretty stellar images and videos in the process. A new study out of the Harvard and Smithsonian Center for Astrophysics introduces Lumina, which provides an unprecedented look at how the universe may have formed. The simulation harkens back to the nascent universe, from the dark ages that followed the Big Bang through the next 2 billion years of cosmic evolution. “The early universe has become an exciting new frontier in astrophysics,” lead author Oliver Zier said in a statement , crediting the James Webb scope. “To understand what we are seeing with this telescope, we need to translate our theories into detailed predictions. After several years of work, with plenty of ups and downs, it is incredibly rewarding to see the simulation results and watch our predictions come to life in video.” Lumina collaboration A visualization of hydrogen re-ionization Those predictions focus on how the first galaxies, stars, and other cosmic structures were able to form amid a period of total darkness. Per a press release from MIT, the effect of the Big Bang was such that no light or radiation could pass through the “shroud” of neutral hydrogen created by the rapid expansion event. Eventually, however, two massive transformations occurred: the re-ionization of hydrogen and the re-ionization of helium. Hydrogen re-ionization refers to the era when the first stars were able to emit enough ultraviolet light to strip the neutral hydrogen of its electrons, preventing it from absorbing photons and thus “allowing light to travel freely.” Similarly, helium re-ionization refers to the breaking apart of neutral helium via high-energy light, something thought to have been fueled by supermassive black holes. The simulation captures these two essential processes in detail for the first time. Lumina collaboration A visualization of helium re-ionization “Lumina does everything from small-scale star and galaxy formation to large-scale re-ionization of hydrogen and helium, in a volume that is 100 times larger than previous best simulations,” study co-author Mark Vogelsberger said in the press release. He added the detail is unparalleled: “Other simulations cannot zoom in as far as this. The difference between the smallest and largest scales that we simulate is larger than in any other simulation.” Looking ahead, the team is making Lumina available to the scientific community to compare its simulations with real-world snapshots taken by new and future telescopes and tell a more complete story of how the first galaxies, stars, and structures of the universe may have formed. items.descriptionOriginal: Bengaluru has a strange paradox: a city that floods every monsoon still struggles with water shortages. Watching its lakes disappear beneath concrete and waste, Harsha Tej decided to do something about it. He quit his job, picked up a shovel and began restoring the water bodies that once gave the city life. Through the BlueDot Foundation, Harsha has helped restore 18 lakes across Karnataka and plant more than 1.5 lakh native trees. From clearing invasive growth to rebuilding habitats, his work goes beyond beautifying lakes. Healthy lakes can support wildlife, help recharge groundwater and improve the landscape’s ability to manage rainwater. For Harsha, every restored lake brings Bengaluru a step closer to the city he remembers, where nature and urban life coexist. His journey shows how one person’s determination can inspire meaningful environmental change, one lake at a time. Can restoring our lakes help build a more water-secure Bengaluru? #WaterConservation #SolvedInIndia #KarnatakaLakes #GroundwaterRecharge #BengaluruLakes #LakeRestoration #Bengaluru #TheBetterIndia

items.title: Από ένα πρόβλημα ταξινόμησης του 1972 στο DIGIPIN: Η ιστορία πίσω από τους 6-ψήφιους κωδικούς PIN της Ινδίας
items.titleOriginal: From a 1972 Sorting Problem to DIGIPIN: The Story Behind India’s 6-digit PIN Codes
items.description: Μια επιστολή για επιστήμονες στον ερευνητικό σταθμό Maitri της Ινδίας στην Ανταρκτική φέρει τον ίδιο κωδικό PIN με το Panaji , 403001, επειδή το πολικό ταχυδρομείο ταξιδεύει μέσω του Εθνικού Κέντρου Πολικής και Ωκεανικής Έρευνας στο Vasco στη Γκόα. Η ιδιορρυθμία δείχνει πόση δουλειά κάνουν οι έξι αριθμοί για τα ταχυδρομεία 1,64 lakh που λειτουργεί σήμερα η India Post και την ιστορία αυτού…
items.descriptionOriginal: A letter for scientists at India's Maitri research station in Antarctica carrie the same PIN code as Panaji , 403001, because polar mail travels through the National Centre for Polar and Ocean Research at Vasco in Goa. The quirk shows how much work six numerals do for the 1.64 lakh post offices that India Post operates today, and the story of that code begins with a sorting problem more than 50 years old. A country of similar place names At Independence in 1947, India had 23,344 post offices, mostly in cities, but the network had to keep pace with a growing country. The Postal Index Number, introduced on 15 August, 1972, aimed to ease the sorting and delivery of mail in a land where different places often share the same or similar names and letters arrive in a wide variety of languages. The idea came from Shriram Bhikaji Velankar, an additional secretary in the Ministry of Communications and a senior member of the Posts and Telegraphs Board. Velankar also wrote Sanskrit poetry, received the President's Award for Sanskrit in 1996, chaired the Indipex stamp exhibition in New Delhi in 1973, and retired from government service on 31 December, 1973. What each of the six digits tells you The length follows from the hierarchy of the code, which gives one digit to the zone, one to the sub-region, one to the sorting district, and three to the delivery post office. The first digit names one of eight regional zones, running from 1 for Delhi, Haryana, Punjab and Himachal Pradesh to 8 for Bihar and Jharkhand, while 9 belongs to the Army Postal Service. Photograph: ( Hindustan Times /AI-Generated collage) The second digit narrows the zone to a sub-region, and the third, read together with the first two, marks a sorting district headquartered at the main post office of the largest city in the area. Goa's 403 carves out a small piece of the 40 to 44 band that otherwise belongs to Maharashtra. The final three digits identify the delivery office, and a busy office that splits in two receives the next available code. Each PIN maps to exactly one delivery post office, which receives the mail for every sub-office and branch office in its jurisdiction. A single PIN code can therefore cover a cluster of villages, and two neighbouring delivery offices share only their first four digits. The same code at the edges of the map The structure holds even at altitude, where the post office in Hikkim, a Spiti Valley village , stands at 4,400 metres and closes for six months each winter when snow cuts off the settlement. Its code, 172114, places it in Himachal Pradesh through the prefix 17, and the office ranks among the highest in the world. The floating post office on Dal Lake began as a postal boat in 1953. It belongs to the same national network as any city head post office. Photograph: ( Lifeandtrendz ) The system also reaches Dal Lake in Srinagar, where the floating post office , which began as a postal boat serving lake communities in 1953, belongs to the same national network as any city head post office. The ninth zone serves a different kind of address, because the Army Postal Service runs field post offices serving the Army, Navy and Air Force across the country. The 2017 Salute a Soldier campaign, organised by India Post and the Postcrossing Society of India in Bengaluru, directed postcards of thanks to around 1,000 Army units. Why six digits still matter The model has a precedent abroad, because the United States introduced its Zone Improvement Plan code on 1 July, 1963, when letters passed through about 17 sorting stops. India followed nine years later with a hierarchy of its own, and its relevance remains clear whenever someone orders food or a parcel online. India Post has since added DIGIPIN, a 10-character code developed with IIT Hyderabad and ISRO that identifies a 4 m by 4 m square, and it complements the six-digit code rather than replacing it. The PIN still tells a sorter which zone, district and office should handle a letter, while DIGIPIN tells a delivery person which doorstep to find. Anyone can check a code using the lookup on India Post's website, and no PIN begins with 0, because the nine zones run from 1 to 9. Taken together, the digits turn an address into a route. A PIN such as 403001 tells a sorter that the mail belongs to the western zone, Goa's sorting district and the Panaji head office, and it does so without a word of any local language. That efficiency, which began on 15 August, 1972, still reaches from the largest cities to the highest hamlets. Sources ' Government expands postal network with 10,170 post offices over last 11 years ': by All India Radio News, Published on 10 December, 2025 ' What is DIGIPIN, India's new high-tech address system from Dept of Posts? ': By The Week, Published on 31 May, 2025

items.descriptionOriginal: People are drowning in eco-friendly swag—cloth tote bags, reusable water bottles, recycled notebooks, sustainable hotel toiletries, and on and on—distributed by organizations and companies eager to demonstrate their environmental bona fides. What might be even more sustainable than manufacturing and distributing all these eco-friendly products is to just…stop. The trouble is that consumers have trouble giving brands credit for such restraint, a quirk of human psychology that researchers dub “sustainable additive bias” in a new paper. “Companies that genuinely try to take eco-friendly actions, such as reducing packaging or promotional giveaways, are often not rewarded,” says study team member Linda Lemarié , associate professor of marketing at Audencia Business School in France. “What we don’t see is hard to take into consideration, and reduction leaves nothing visible, even though it’s often the best strategy from an environmental standpoint.” In the paper, Lemarié and her colleagues conducted nine different studies to demonstrate how this bias works—and what companies can do about it. The studies included a field experiment in which hotel guests rated the sustainability of the room they had stayed in, a lab experiment in which business school students chose gifts to hand out to trade show attendees, and seven online investigations in which a total of more than 2,900 participants were asked to evaluate complimentary hotel toiletries, hair care sets, music festival welcome bags, and other collections of products. Overall, the studies show that consumers see businesses as more sustainable when they provide more eco-friendly items rather than when they remove unnecessary ones—even though subtracting can lead to true: Information that confirms your beliefs...or information repeated over and over? “We were first surprised by the robustness and consistency of the effect across different contexts and with different metrics,” Lemarié says. For example, study participants judged a hotel room stocked with a large selection of eco-friendly toiletries as more sustainable than a room with a more modest set of eco-friendly products. They also judged a limited-edition tea box to which eco-friendly tea filters had been added as more sustainable than one from which they had been removed. “Then we were also surprised by the bias’s resistance to knowledge,” Lemarié says. When items weren’t labeled as being environmentally friendly , participants identified bundles with more items as being less sustainable than those with fewer. “This means that people do indeed correctly associate ‘addition with ‘less environmentally friendly.’” But when the question of sustainability comes into play, people seem to use visible components as indicators of companies’ effort. The more items, the more effort, and the more effort, the more sustainability—at least, according to our imperfect brains. Several of the experiments suggest sustainable additive bias can be counteracted when companies prioritize highly recognizable items as sustainability signals (that is, a refillable water bottle counts more than biodegradable glitter). One hints that explaining when items have been removed for environmental reasons might help, too. But accomplishing this in the real world could be tricky, Lemarié says. “The question our research leaves open is how to effectively demonstrate, without appearing hypocritical or making people skeptical, that reducing elements of a product offering, and thus offering less, is a genuine effort in favor of the environment.” Source: Lemarié L. et al. “ The more, the better? items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News Blue-Green Corridor Transforms a Flood-Prone Waterway in Thimphu in Bhutan Reading Time: 3 minutes Bhutan’s capital is transforming the flood-prone Memorial Chorten stream into a blue-green corridor that combines flood protection, ecological restoration, and inclusive public space. A new blue-green corridor is taking shape along Thimphu’s Memorial Chorten stream in Bhutan. City planners want to turn the flood-prone waterway into a safer, greener public space. The stream flows past some of the capital’s most visited landmarks. The Memorial Chorten stream is one of five key waterways identified in Thimphu’s long-term city plan . It connects the city center to the Wang Chhu River. Rapid construction and heavier rains have made the corridor increasingly prone to flooding. The stream passes near the National Memorial Chorten, a well-known Buddhist stupa in the capital. It also runs by the Royal Bhutan Police Headquarters and the Changlimithang area. Despite this central location, much of the corridor remains hard to access today. Queen Ashi Phuntsho Choden Wangchuck built the Memorial Chorten decades ago in memory of the third king. Today it stands as one of Bhutan’s most visited religious sites. Its surrounding stream corridor sees heavy foot traffic from residents and visitors alike. Flooding has become a growing concern across Thimphu in recent years. A flash flood tore through the nearby Dechencholing community in 2025. Officials say the city, originally planned for a much smaller population, now faces mounting climate pressure. Thimphu Thromde, the city’s municipal government, has now finalized a revitalization design plan for the site. The project blends engineered flood controls with nature-based solutions to build a blue-green corridor. Together, these measures aim to lower flood risk while restoring the stream’s ecological health. Planned work includes restoring riparian plants and naturalizing the stream channel itself. New retention ponds would capture stormwater before it floods nearby streets. Waste interception systems would also help keep pollution out of the waterway. New walking trails, viewing areas, and solar-powered lighting would open the future blue-green corridor to the public. Better pedestrian paths are also expected to improve safety around the stream. Recreational spaces are planned to encourage residents to spend time outdoors. Thimphu’s planned blue-green corridor will combine naturalized stream channels, stormwater retention ponds, and waste interception systems with solar-powered walking trails, viewing areas, and recreational spaces, turning a flood-prone urban waterway into a safe, accessible public amenity. Photo by Dechen Wangmo, courtesy of UNDP . Inclusive design guided much of the planning process from the start. Planners want the corridor to feel safe and accessible for women, children, and older residents. The site’s design also considered people with disabilities. The design plan came together through the Disaster Resilient Infrastructure Project. The United Nations Development Programme (UNDP) supported the effort. Funding came through the Coalition for Disaster Resilient Infrastructure, or CDRI, and its Infrastructure Resilience Accelerator Fund. A separate ongoing initiative will help carry the design into construction. That project, backed by UNDP and the Global Environment Facility, focuses on wider urban climate resilience. Reports indicate Bhutan has allocated roughly $24 million toward related stream corridor work. That broader initiative also covers more than 30 kilometers of stormwater drains across central Thimphu. The Global Environment Facility and the Royal Government of Bhutan jointly fund the six-year effort. Together, these projects mark one of the largest urban resilience pushes in the country’s history. Engineers, landscape architects, and gender specialists all contributed to the design. Local agencies held site assessments and community consultations before finalizing plans. That collaborative process shaped decisions on everything from drainage to lighting. Officials describe the effort as one of Bhutan’s first projects to combine several goals at once. Disaster resilience, ecological restoration, and inclusive public space design all come together in a single corridor. Few urban projects in the region have attempted such an integrated approach. The project supports goals set out in Bhutan’s National Adaptation Plan. It also echoes the country’s long-term strategy for low-emission, climate-resilient development . Urban human settlements remain a key focus area under both documents. Officials hope the corridor can serve as a practical model for other Bhutanese cities facing similar flood risks and growing pressure on urban waterways. Lessons from Thimphu could soon help guide blue-green corridor projects along other rivers and streams, showing how restoring natural waterways can strengthen urban resilience while creating healthier public spaces. For a small mountain kingdom, restoring one stream could provide valuable lessons and help protect many more communities from future flooding. The post Blue-Green Corridor Transforms a Flood-Prone Waterway in Thimphu in Bhutan appeared first on Happy Eco News .

items.descriptionOriginal: P atty Spillman and her husband farm over 400 acres of corn, soybeans and wheat in central Ohio. Both have lived in the area all their lives; his family has been on the land since 1861. In 2023, a developer proposed a data center on a nearby farm. “[The community] fought them off,” she says. “But I always kind of knew that just because the one data center had left, that didn’t mean it was going to be gone forever. Someone else was going to be right on their heels.” She was right. Less than two years later, another developer started moving forward with plans for a much larger data center, located across the street from her farm. Headwaters, a Texas-based company, wanted to annex land in Pleasant Township (where Spillman lives) and nearby Jackson Township for a 300-plus acre facility in Grove City. This is a story playing out in communities across the U.S., where A.I. demands have rapidly accelerated the need for data centers, along with the extraordinary amounts of water and energy that they consume. But residents are pushing back, advocating for more community input, insisting that the data facilities cover the full cost of locating there (such as local grid infrastructure upgrades), and even calling for outright moratoriums. Patty Spillman and her husband on their land. Courtesy of Protect Grove City Crucially, these movements don’t break along party lines: Republicans, Democrats and Independents across the country are mad — and they’re working together to block development. This bipartisan push is particularly notable at a time of intense polarization. There’s not much that people from different political parties can agree on, but according to a recent poll from the University of Massachusetts Amherst, very few people want an A.I. data center in their community. That’s certainly true in Grove City, a Republican-leaning suburb of Columbus, where people of all parties opposed the Headwaters development. The nature of this coalition isn’t totally unprecedented, says Megan Mullin, a professor of public policy at the University of California, Los Angeles. “In so many ways, data center battles look like land use battles that have come before,” she says. “Battles over housing developments, wind farms or gas pipelines — we consistently see people come together across party lines to try to keep their community looking the way it’s always looked, and to fight back against what they perceive as harmful draws on community resources.” Mullin says a big difference now is that all of these hyper-local fights are happening at once. While one or two bipartisan coalitions on a land use debate wouldn’t rise to the level of national news, hundreds of them happening simultaneously around the country does. “That allows these local disputes to be connected to something national, and it also allows concrete movement building.” Weighed down by negative news? Enter your email below to receive our smart, uplifting newsletters. Or click here to choose exactly which ones you want [contact-form-7] In Ohio, residents of Grove City and the surrounding townships quickly mobilized once they realized that Headwaters wanted to site a data center in their community. “We got organized,” says Jen Belt, one of the four people behind Protect Grove City , which actively opposed the development. “Most people weren’t even aware that this was a thing. We taped flyers to every home within a three-mile radius of the developer’s site. We encouraged people to come to all of the council meetings.” They also worked on gathering signatures to encourage the Grove City city council to pass a moratorium. (Pleasant Township and Jackson Township had already passed moratoriums in the first half of 2026.) Ultimately, Belt says, they gathered more than 4,000 signatures for the online petition. Their efforts worked. In June, the city council passed a one-year moratorium on data center development. But Belt and her neighbors know it is temporary, and developers will come back once the year is up. So they have put a Community Consent Amendment (CCA) on the upcoming November ballot. If passed, it will require residents’ approval before any large-scale development can break ground. (While it’s geared toward data centers, it’s written to apply to all heavy industry.) Belt, like Spillman, lives in Pleasant Township, which she calls “suburban rural.” But she scoffs at the idea that the issue doesn’t impact her just because she’s not within city limits. “This is property that will be annexed from my town into Grove City,” says Belt, a registered Democrat. “It’s literally in my backyard. So it does affect us.” Spillman, a lifelong Republican, agrees: “This is our community. This is our neighborhood, and none of us can vote on any of this, because we don’t live in Grove City proper, but we still consider Grove City our home.” Data centers have been going up in earnest for the last decade, built to support the rapid growth of the cloud. Opposition has existed nearly as long . But as A.I. usage has exploded in the last several years, the demand for data centers has rapidly accelerated as well. The post Finally, Something Americans Agree On! appeared first on Reasons to be Cheerful .

items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News How Urban Woodlands and Mental Health are Connected, According to a Major Scottish Study Reading Time: 3 minutes A major five-year study finds that urban woodlands and mental health are closely connected, with well-kept city woods linked to fewer antidepressant prescriptions in Scotland’s poorest neighborhoods. Urban woodlands and mental health appear to move together, according to new research from the Universities of Edinburgh and Glasgow. Scientists tracked more than 129,000 people across Scotland over five years. They found that people living close to improved woodlands used less medication for depression and anxiety. The study , published in The Lancet Planetary Health, used National Health Service prescription records alongside census data. Researchers compared people living within a 10-minute walk of an upgraded woodland to those living farther away. The gap in medication use was substantial. People near a well-maintained, welcoming woodland were 10% less likely to be prescribed antidepressants. They were also 6% less likely to need anti-anxiety medication. That pattern held even after researchers accounted for income, demographics, and other factors known to affect mental health. This is one of the largest studies of its kind linking urban woodlands and mental health outcomes. The woodland upgrades came through Scottish Forestry’s Woods In and Around Towns program (WIAT). Funding paid for new footpaths, better signage, and community events in areas that needed it most. The program specifically targeted socially and financially disadvantaged communities. These are often the places with the least access to quality parks and green space to begin with. By focusing improvements there, researchers could measure whether fixing a woodland actually changed people’s health, not just their surroundings. What makes this research especially convincing is how it tracked people over time. When someone moved closer to an improved woodland, their need for medication tended to drop. When they moved farther away, that protective effect faded. The connection between urban woodlands and mental health was strengthened with a telling finding: when people moved closer to improved woodlands, their need for antidepressants fell, and when they moved away, the protective effect faded with them. Photo by Vitaly Gariev on Pexels. That detail matters. Earlier studies often compared different people living in different neighborhoods at a single moment. This approach made it hard to know whether nature improved mental health, or whether healthier people simply chose to live near woodlands already. By following the same individuals as their circumstances changed, researchers could rule out that explanation. Professor Catharine Ward Thompson, who led the study at the University of Edinburgh’s OPENspace Research Centre, said the findings offer stronger evidence on the link between urban woodlands and mental health than earlier research managed to provide. She added that the benefits may help reduce mental health inequalities across the population. Dr. Scott Ogletree, who carried out the analysis, said the project marks the first time mental health service data has been linked to a long-term national urban forestry program. He noted that relatively modest investments in local green space can meaningfully improve people’s wellbeing. Nature-based programs like WIAT, he said, can support broader efforts to improve mental health. The scale of the problem makes this evidence timely. Around one in eight people worldwide live with a mental health condition, and people in poorer communities are often hit hardest. These same communities often have the least access to high-quality woodlands and parks. Scotland’s government has pointed to this research as support for its wider environmental goals. Officials cited a target of creating 18,000 hectares of new woodland every year by 2029 to 2030. That commitment extends to urban tree planting aimed at improving air quality and quality of life. The connection between urban woodlands and mental health also fits into a broader pattern seen elsewhere, where community-driven tree planting has helped cool neighborhoods and improve public health by giving residents a direct role in restoring local green space. Programs like these suggest the benefits of investing in trees extend well beyond any single country. The research team behind the Scottish study has spent more than 20 years gathering evidence on the social value of local woodlands, working alongside Scottish Forestry and Forest Research. Their latest findings add a rigorous, long-term dataset to a growing conversation about nature-based public health policy. Funding came from the Economic and Social Research Council and the GroundsWell Consortium, a UK research partnership focused on how green and blue spaces reduce health inequalities. None of this suggests woodlands replace clinical care for depression or anxiety. What it does suggest is that a safe, welcoming patch of trees within walking distance can meaningfully shift the odds. As more cities weigh where to spend limited public money, the growing evidence on urban woodlands and mental health makes a strong case for choosing the trail over the parking lot. The post How Urban Woodlands and Mental Health are Connected, According to a Major Scottish Study appeared first on Happy Eco News .

items.descriptionOriginal: What happens when two generations open their doors to one another? In West Philadelphia, a small but growing program called Second Story Collective is bringing college students and older residents together through shared housing, creating unexpected friendships along the way. For Ms. Julia, a retired nursing assistant who has lived in her neighborhood for more than 50 years, welcoming 22-year-old Drexel University student Jackson Tignor into her home has brought new companionship and laughter. In return, Jackson has found more than an affordable place to live -- he's discovered a sense of belonging and a deeper connection to the community around him. Through everyday moments of shared meals, conversations, and helping hands, the program is quietly challenging loneliness, housing insecurity, and the divisions that too often separate generations. Sometimes, building a stronger community begins with something as simple as opening a door.

items.descriptionOriginal: BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM Most people moving through a train station aren’t really paying attention. They’re somewhere between where they left and where they’re going, phone out, eyes on the platform. Putting art there is an interesting bet; you’re trying to get someone to stop and look at something that might surprise and delight them, and that they had no intention of seeking out. NJ Transit has been doing this since 2019, when it launched the TRANSITional Art Project as a pilot at Newark Penn Station. Working with the New Jersey State Council on the Arts , it has since installed temporary exhibitions of murals and photography by New Jersey artists at seven more stations. The latest is now at Morris Plains Rail Station: a show called “ Tracks Through Time: Movement, History and Human Connection .” A show about the tracks themselves The subject matter has good timing. The exhibition looks at 250 years of American history through the lens of railroads , in the very stations where people still depend on those rails to get to work. It includes photography by Beyti Barbaros, murals by Jonathan Yumi, and a three-panel mural installation by Catherine Thurston. “Railroads helped to build this nation,” said NJ Transit President and CEO Kris Kolluri, “and as we mark 250 years of our shared history, there’s no better place to tell that story than in the very stations where the past and daily life intersect.” Art you don’t have to go looking for Nobody goes to a train station specifically to see art, but that might be at the heart of the reasoning for this whole project. Most people at a gallery already decided they wanted to be there. The commuter who glances up at a mural while waiting for the 8:14 didn’t, and that’s a different kind of encounter. Danielle Bursk, the New Jersey State Arts Council Director of Community Partnerships & Artist Services, put it this way: “Public art has the power to transform the places we move through every day into places where we can pause, connect , and see our communities in new ways.” The program also pays the artists. Some participants receive stipends toward the cost of developing a project in a transit space, which matters given how rarely public art comes with any budget at all. The program has now reached eight stations: Newark, Camden, Atlantic City, Trenton, New Brunswick, Summit, Rahway, and Morris Plains. Did this solution stand out? Share it with a friend or support our mission by becoming an Emissary . The post New Jersey Transit is turning commuter stations into art galleries first appeared on The Optimist Daily: Making Solutions the News .

items.descriptionOriginal: BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM Researchers at Columbia University Medical Center wanted to answer a specific question: what is the least amount of movement needed to offset the effects of prolonged sitting ? In 2023, they tested a range of options and found that walking for five minutes every 30 minutes was the most effective strategy. Not a longer walk once an hour. Not standing more. The answer was as short and sweet as five minutes, every half hour. When NPR’s Body Electric ran that same challenge with more than 20,000 listeners, participants reported higher productivity and lower fatigue. Those results have real implications: adults in the United States average 9.5 hours of sitting per day, and the research linking prolonged sitting to fatigue, weight gain, back pain , and chronic disease is extensive. The five-minute walk is the most surprising and accessible finding, but there are four other adjustments, drawn from physical therapists, a biomechanist, and a professional ergonomist, that address what walking breaks alone can’t fix. For back pain: a three-dimensional spine rotation Slouching at a desk doesn’t just feel uncomfortable; it puts sustained stress on the middle section of the spine. Vinh Pham , a physical therapist, recommends a move he calls the 3D T-spine rotation. Stand and drop your right foot behind your left, about a foot apart. Hold your right arm straight up and your left arm behind you, as if shaking the hand of someone behind you. Then simultaneously drop both arms and twist toward your right foot, keeping them straight throughout. Return to the starting position, hold for two seconds, and repeat ten times before switching sides. The goal isn’t stretching in the conventional sense. It’s to get the spine comfortable with its full range of motion — side bending, backward bending, rotating — so those movements don’t cause pain when they come up in ordinary life. For eye strain: look somewhere else Digital eye strain happens when the eyes spend hours focused at close range. They turn inward to track a nearby screen, adjust their focus for short vision, and hold that position. Eye doctors say the result is often fatigue, headaches, or blurred vision. The simplest intervention is the one most people already know and skip: look away from the screen and focus on something distant. A full eye-muscle stretch goes further. That means moving your gaze deliberately through different positions to work muscles that stay locked during screen time . For restlessness: stop trying to find the right posture Katy Bowman , a biomechanist and author of Rethink Your Position , is direct on the idea that fidgeting is a signal, not a bad habit. It means your body needs to stop holding a static position, regardless of how ergonomically correct that position might be. Bowman and physical therapist Leada Malek , author of Science of Stretch , share a phrase common in their field: “Your best posture is your next posture.” Any position, held long enough, creates strain. The goal isn’t to find the correct one and maintain it; it’s to keep moving between positions. Sitting, standing, reclining, shifting. “Adaptive and dynamic,” as Malek describes it, and easy to move in and out of. For shoulder and neck aches: fix the monitor height first Professional ergonomist Meg Honan identifies one setup problem that causes more widespread discomfort than almost anything else: the “head down, arms up” configuration, where the screen is too low and the keyboard is too high. Bring your screen to eye level using books, a stand, or whatever is available. Lower your keyboard and mouse so you’re not shrugging to type. If your keyboard is attached to your laptop, an external keyboard lets you lower your arms without losing screen height. Honan describes the head-down, arms-up position as a reliable setup for feeling “achy, sore and tired.” Getting the monitor to eye level is the single adjustment with the most downstream effect. Did this solution stand out? Share it with a friend or support our mission by becoming an Emissary . The post 5 research-backed ways to banish aches and feel better at your desk first appeared on The Optimist Daily: Making Solutions the News .

items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News 5 Sustainable Swaps You Can Make Around Your Home Today Reading Time: 2 minutes 5 Sustainable Swaps You Can Make Around Your Home Today Making your home more sustainable doesn’t require expensive renovations or a complete lifestyle overhaul. In fact, some of the most effective changes are surprisingly simple, and you can start making them today. From the products you use to clean your kitchen to the materials you sleep under, everyday household choices can affect the environment. If you want to reduce waste, embrace more natural materials, and make your home a little greener, here are five sustainable swaps to consider. 1. Swap Disposable Cleaning Products for Reusable Alternatives Consider how many paper towels, disposable wipes, and plastic cleaning bottles you use in a typical month. These everyday essentials can create surprising waste, especially when you replace them constantly. Instead, consider switching to washable microfiber cloths, reusable cleaning pads, and refillable spray bottles . You can also explore concentrated cleaning solutions that require less packaging and are designed to be diluted at home. These small changes can reduce household waste while helping you save money over time. 2. Choose Natural Bedding Over Synthetic Materials Your bedroom is another great place to introduce more sustainable materials, especially in your bedding. Many conventional comforters contain synthetic polyester fillings derived from petroleum-based materials, which can contribute to plastic pollution. Replacing them with natural alternatives is a more environmentally conscious choice. An organic wool comforter offers a natural filling that provides warmth while allowing air to circulate and helping regulate temperature throughout the night. Wool is also renewable and biodegradable when untreated, making it an appealing option for anyone looking to reduce reliance on synthetic textiles. Your bedroom is a great place to introduce sustainable materials, especially in your bedding. Image: Home of Wool 3. Replace Single-Use Kitchen Products The kitchen is often one of the biggest sources of household waste, but it’s also one of the easiest places to make sustainable improvements. Instead of relying on plastic wrap, disposable sandwich bags, and single-use food containers, invest in reusable alternatives. Glass storage containers, washable silicone bags, and beeswax food wraps can help you cut down on unnecessary packaging. You could also swap disposable coffee pods for a reusable coffee filter or French press. Over time, these changes can noticeably reduce how much waste leaves your kitchen. 4. Switch to Energy-Efficient Lighting If you’re still using traditional incandescent light bulbs, switching to LED alternatives is a straightforward way to reduce household energy consumption. LED bulbs use significantly less electricity and generally last much longer than incandescent bulbs, so you need to replace them less often. This can help lower both your electricity bills and your home’s environmental footprint. You can also make better use of natural daylight by keeping windows unobstructed and arranging furniture to maximize available sunlight. 5. Choose Refillable Bathroom Essentials Bathrooms can quickly accumulate plastic packaging, particularly from shampoo, conditioner, hand soap, and body wash bottles. Switch to refillable products or solid alternatives, such as shampoo bars and bar soaps. Many brands now offer concentrated refills, so you can reuse existing containers instead of buying new plastic bottles every time. You might also replace disposable cotton rounds with washable alternatives and choose toothbrushes with replaceable heads to cut unnecessary waste. Start with one or two manageable swaps, build on them gradually, and you’ll soon discover that sustainable living can be both practical and rewarding. The post 5 Sustainable Swaps You Can Make Around Your Home Today appeared first on Happy Eco News .

items.descriptionOriginal: E very few weeks, Jackie Jantzi sits in on school board meetings in Akron, Ohio, taking notes on her laptop. Afterward, she polishes a summary of what happened, to be published online, free for anyone to read. Jantzi is there working for local news website Signal Akron , but she isn’t a professional reporter. She’s one of hundreds of city residents deployed by the news outlet to record what happens at local government meetings, through a program called Documenters . The write-ups they produce don’t just help the news outlet cover far more than would otherwise be possible with its staff of six reporters; they also create a public record where Akronites can follow the nitty gritty of the local decisions shaping their community. “National politics feels like you have zero power, you know? It just feels so big and out of your hands,” Jantzi says. “But any sort of civic engagement, like Documenters or even getting to know your neighbors, gives you a little bit of power locally.” As thousands of local news outlets have shrunk or shuttered , many Americans have lost reliable sources of information about municipal budget negotiations and school board votes. In their stead, national news has comprised a larger share of the public’s media diet, drawing attention to partisan divides and widening political polarization. By spotlighting community level issues, local news sources are finding ways to invigorate interest around what’s happening in their communities, helping people to refocus on public decision-making in their own backyards — which tends to fall less along the national red-blue divide. A Documenter on assignment in Chicago. Credit: City Bureau “When people have a chance to be able to talk about politics with nuance, to talk about how decisions that are being made in government affect their neighborhoods and communities, it drastically changes the types of conversations that folks have about things like health care, like access to food, like immigration,” says Max Resnik, who is helping to grow a network of 25 local Documenters programs across the country. Local news has suffered for the last three decades amid competition for attention — first from cable news, then the internet and now social media, explains Johanna Dunaway, a professor of political science at Syracuse University. As revenue dropped, outlets invested less in their newsrooms, leaving diminished staff capacity to report on towns and neighborhoods. In 2002, for every 100,000 Americans, there were 40 journalists covering local news . Today, the rate works out to 7.8. In many places, entire outlets have disappeared. Almost 40 percent of local newspapers have closed since 2005, and about one in seven Americans now live in counties with only one or no source of local news. Weighed down by negative news? Enter your email below to receive our smart, uplifting newsletters. Or click here to choose exactly which ones you want [contact-form-7] Those closures have been shown to have a significant effect on political division. In a study assessing the relationship between newspaper closures and polarized voting, Dunaway and colleagues found that split-ticket voting — when people vote for candidates of different parties on the same ballot — decreased by a small but notable 1.9 percent in communities that had lost a newspaper before the 2012 election. A factor driving polarization, she explains, is that Americans’ attention has shifted to the national stage. “Most of the political news stories are framed in terms of the parties waging wars against each other,” says Dunaway, “whereas local news is more about the issues that face your school district, your garbage collection, the potholes, traffic — things that are less partisan in nature.” Dunaway’s study of voting patterns caught the eye of Julie Makinen, then-executive editor of the Desert Sun newspaper in southern California. Makinen launched an experiment: For a month, the opinion section ditched syndicated columns and letters about national disputes for locally authored commentaries and California-focused political cartoons. Credit: City Bureau “Local news gives people so many different touch points to connect with people in their community.” —Julie Makinen The test provided a living lab for Dunaway and her colleagues. They found that removing national politics from the opinion section didn’t reverse polarization in the Palm Springs region, but it did slow down feelings of distance between people of different political positions. The exact cause of this is unclear, according to Dunaway. Is it from increasing attention on less ideologically divided local issues? Or reducing consumption of national, more partisan news? But one of the clearest insights, she says, is that it’s viable for publications to reduce national news coverage. “People had opinions and complaints, but they, on the whole, were mostly glad to see less national stuff and more local.” For Makinen, the experience speaks to the importance of forums for civil discussion about local issues. And the community seemed to agree. When Gannett, the paper’s owner, discontinued the opinion section, community members worked with Makinen to raise money to continue to pay for an opinion editor. That fundraising effort became the Coachella Valley Journalism Foundation , a nonprofit that now supports newsrooms across the region with trainings, awards and funding for newsroom jobs. The stories local outlets cover about what’s happening at the city and county level have a much bigger impact on people’s lives than the national stage, Makinen notes. And, they create openings where community members can build relationships with each other. “Local news gives people so many different touch points to connect with people in their community, and sort of feel less isolated and polarized,” she says. Documenters is one way local news is helping community members find those touch points. The approach to citizen journalism was developed in Chicago by the nonprofit news outlet City Bureau, when the editorial team decided to recruit residents to help comb through a massive police document. It would have taken one reporter dozens of hours alone, explains Resnik. But by bringing in residents interested in flexing their research muscles, the outlet expanded its capacity and built new relationships with the community. Participants at a Documenters training session. Credit: City Bureau That evolved into Documenters, a model Resnik describes as a “civic side hustle,” where community members are paid a stipend to, as he says, “commit these small acts of journalism.” The approach has since been adopted in 25 communities, each run locally by a news or civic organization. In Ohio, Signal Akron launched three years ago simultaneously with their Documenters program, building the network of residents into the way the publication operates. Each week, community editor Kevin Dilley recruits from a pool of more than 400 trained Documenters to cover about a dozen local meetings. Documenters apply to cover meetings as fits their schedule, and make about $90 per meeting. They write up summaries, highlighting a few points they find most important. After some light editing, summaries are posted on the Documenters Akron website. If something particularly noteworthy happens, the summary may get published on Signal Akron’s main website, alongside stories written by the outlet’s professional journalists. The program, according to Dilley, has resulted in an extraordinarily diverse newsroom. Documenters range in age from 19 to 84, some with PhDs, others reentering from incarceration. Every zip code in the greater Akron area is represented. For Dilley, this community-driven approach provides an opportunity to rebuild trust in local news. Residents may be skeptical of news media, and even of Signal Akron. “Here’s the thing with the Documenters,” he says. “You trust your neighbors.” One of the biggest challenges is funding. In Akron, there are more public meetings — and more Documenters interested in covering them — than the small editorial team can handle. Dunaway, of Syracuse University, notes that there is a resurgence of attention on local news. With the internet, many anticipated that online sources about hyperlocal news issues would naturally emerge, but it didn’t happen. Now, she notes, there are concerted efforts to boost local news coverage in order to fill the need. So far, however, she says they tend to be scattershot. Urban areas tend to be better served, while rural and lower-income communities are less well-covered. Wait, you're not a member yet? Join the Reasons to be Cheerful community by supporting our nonprofit publication and giving what you can. Join Cancel anytime What exactly local news looks like is also changing. Across the country, Documenters share information through messaging networks, bulletin boards and conversations with neighbors. And instead of framing local elections in the national two-party horserace, Documenters have focused on making sure community members understand the roles of the municipal positions on the ballot. “It changes this idea of an ‘us v. them’ into something where there’s much, much more nuance,” Resnik says. Jantzi believes every community should have something like a Documenters program. It’s not that local politics aren’t divisive, she says. Police issues tend to be highly polarized, and school board meetings get so contentious they stretch for hours. But by seeing meetings play out, and connecting with neighbors who are interested, there’s more awareness of the nuances of local governance. “There’s just more accountability for the decision-making and more power to the community to actually learn what’s happening,” she says. The post Want the News to Unite People? Let Them Report It appeared first on Reasons to be Cheerful .

items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News How Burrowing Owls Nesting on Solar Farms are Rewriting a Species’ Future Reading Time: 3 minutes Burrowing owls nesting on solar farms are showing that clean energy and wildlife habitat can share the same land. Burrowing owls nesting on solar farms are turning a renewable energy site into an unlikely nursery. More than a dozen owlets hatched this summer inside plastic tunnels at a 10,000-acre solar complex near Phoenix, Arizona. The project suggests clean energy and vulnerable wildlife can thrive side by side. Longroad Energy, the solar company that runs the site, teamed up with Wild at Heart , a raptor rehabilitation center. Together they set out to test whether burrowing owls nesting on solar farms could raise families long-term. In March, workers moved nine owl pairs and one single male about 50 miles to the site, since their old burrows were about to be destroyed by new housing. Burrowing owls are small, ground-dwelling birds of prey roughly the size of a loaf of bread, perched on long, stilt-like legs. They typically nest in tunnels dug by animals like ground squirrels and prairie dogs. Since the 1960s, their numbers have dropped by more than a third across the United States. Housing and farmland development keep shrinking that habitat. Conservation groups often relocate colonies before bulldozers arrive, moving them to farmland where they can hunt. But as farmland gets bought up too, safe new sites are harder to find. The Wild at Heart’s Burrowing Owl team had nearly run out of nearby options. They used to drive displaced owls about 50 miles to open farmland. Now some trips stretch 60 to 100 miles, which is too costly to sustain, even though the owls need very little space to settle in. Solar farms offered a new possibility for relocation. Utility-scale solar energy, meaning large power plants built to serve the electric grid, has expanded quickly across Arizona. That growth can squeeze desert wildlife, but it also helps slow climate change, a threat already putting many U.S. bird species at risk. State law required Longroad to survey wildlife before building its Sun Streams project. That survey found eight burrowing owls already living on the land. The discovery connected the company with Wild at Heart, which was running low on relocation space, sparking a larger experiment in burrowing owls nesting on solar farms. Burrowing owls nesting on solar farms emerged as a conservation solution when Longroad Energy’s pre-construction wildlife survey found eight owls already living on the land, connecting the company with Wild at Heart at a moment when the raptor center was running out of relocation space for displaced desert birds. Photo by Greg Clark courtesy of Wild at Heart . After construction finished, Longroad offered Wild at Heart around 250 acres between two Sun Streams projects. Workers installed 40 artificial burrows and placed a breeding pair in each, at first surrounded by netting so the birds would not fly back home. They also set up lights to attract insects and delivered mice daily while the owls adjusted. The company funded feeding and monitoring through the entire breeding season, support Wild at Heart normally cannot afford beyond 30 days. Within one month, every female had laid eggs, an early sign that burrowing owls nesting on solar farms might actually work. By late June, 36 chicks had hatched. Within three months, 29 young owls had fledged and left the nest, and staff slowly stopped feeding them so the birds would learn to hunt on their own. The team began spotting insect remains in their droppings, an encouraging sign. By the end of August, Wild at Heart stopped feedings altogether. Researchers are now studying how to expand this kind of coexistence. A 2025 Arizona State University study found that prime solar sites overlap with burrowing owl habitat by about 13% across seven Western states. The nonprofit Renewable Energy Wildlife Institute is building a database to help solar companies weigh biodiversity when choosing where to build. Arizona is also drafting guidelines to help future solar projects support wildlife instead of displacing it. Wild at Heart hopes to grow vegetation on solar sites to attract insects and rodents for owls to eat, turning relocation sites into lasting habitat. Longroad is even discussing solar panel designs that could capture water from humid air to help plants grow nearby. Small changes like that could make future sites more welcoming for burrowing owls nesting on solar farms from day one. The raptor conservation group hopes to bring more solar companies on board. Burrowing owls nesting on solar farms may soon become less of an experiment and more of a model other developers can copy. If more companies adopt the practice, displaced owl colonies could find lasting homes on the very land built to power their neighbors. For a bird that has lost so much ground, that shift offers a real reason for hope.
